COUNTY OF CHESTER. WILD BIRDS PROTECTION ACTS, 1880, 1894, AND 1896. NOTICE is Hereby Given that the following is a ' copy of an ORDER which has been made by the Right Honourable Sir Matthew White Ridley, Baronet, M.P., Secretary of State for the Home Department viz:— WILD BIRDS (ENGLAND)._
The Wild Birds Protection (County of 'Chester) Order, 1898, Dated 15th February, 1898. . .

In pur3uance of the power 4 conferiea upon me by the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1880 to 1896, and upon appli- cation by the County Council of Chester, I hereby make the following Order, which shall apply to the whole of the County of Chester :- 1. This Order may be cited as "The Wild Birds Pro- tection (County of Chester) Order, 1898." 2. The time during which the killing and taking of wild birds, or any of them, is prohibited by the Wild Birds Protection Aet, 1880 (43 and 44 Vic., cap 35), shall be extended in the County of Chester so as to be from the Ist day of March to the 12th day of August in each year. 3. The Act of 1880, as extended by Section 2of this Order, shall apply within the whole of the County of Chester to the Kestrel and Heron as if those species were included in the Schedule of that Act.

4. The taking or kiting of the following species of birds, namely:—King Fisher,Great Crested Grebe,Heron, Goldfinch and Owl, shall be prohibited within the whole of the County of Chester during the whole of that period of the year to which the protection of wild birds under the Act of 1880 (as extended by Section 2 of this Order) does not extend. 5. The taking or destroyiug of the Eggs of the Owl, the Bittern, the Kingfisher. the Kestrel, the Heron, the Sheldrake,the Dunlin, the Blackheaded Gull,the Common Tern, and the Oyster Catcher, shall be prohibited in the whole of the County of Chester. In tne starlight witn tne lovers- mooa upon tnem, which veils all things tranquilly, they both felt supremely happy, thinking not of the future, rejoicing in the thrilling present. But at parting a feeling of uneasiness possessed the young man. As he bade the girl "Good-night," he pressed her hand tightly, then, imprinting a kiss on her fair cheek, said _ _ _ .

• "This is the longest day, ,my girl, the twenty- first of June. Would that all our days could be as long and full of happiness." He drew her closer, and his voice quivered as he continued: • "I feel, Ella, that we shall part soon; I'm sure we shall. We shall not spend many more nights together." The girl remained quiet as he proceeded.

"I want to see you happy, my girl. I want to let you have all that you wish for. But here it is uphill work getting a little money together.. How long and how hard have we both laboured—for what? For little more than bread and butter. In Africa, my girl, is gold; millions of pounds worth of gold. A few years out there, perhaps not more than one or two, would make my fortune, then I could return here, we could get married and live as well and as comfortably as—as—a factory- master."

It was the best simile that occurred to him. To him, as to the girl at his side, the big house stand- ing in spacious grounds in which his employer resided, was the abode of luxury and comfort. To live in the style of a factory-master was to live regally. His words produced a remarkable effect on his companion. Ella Rayburn's eyes glistened as she conjured up a vision of the good things which would be pro- vided for her when the golden dream was realised. It would be fine t o live in such style, to have a grand house, to Inete servants, mayhap ; to have dresses, and hats, anti all sorts of pretty and stylish things, not alone at Whitsuntide, but just when one wanted them. It would, indeed, be fine! _ _

A year or two would soon pass over; then what a glorious reward for the patient waiting., "But," as she reflected seriously for a moment, it would be hard for Steve. Men had won gold, much gold, but at the cost of much privation and hardship— sometimes at the cost of life itself. And perhaps after all his dream of untold gold might be but a dream, and his labour and trouble would be vain." In any event, gold or no gold, he would have to endure much for her. And she loved him. She had told him that she loved him; she had told herself so, and yet there were times when she half- doubted her feelings towards him. • "Do as you wish, Steve," she said, at parting; "it will be right for me whatever you decide upon."
"Why, I mean Ella Rayburn, the widow's dowter, yo' know, th' bonniest lass in th' mill; yigh, or in Dalesworth." "You are right, Ben; she is a pretty girl." _

- "Pretty girl, say yo? She's-more nor that. She's as good as sh9:s pretty. Her face is her fortune an' her character, too. Any man as would ileave yon lass to go seek t'other sort of a filthy- lucre gowden fortune, is a foo' to hissel, an' Steve Wart is that man." "When do you say he is going, Ben ? " "Next week, I've heard. He's booked his passage awready, they say, an' will sail fro' Lunnon on th' Friday. It's a unlucky day to sail on, an' I'll bet owt it'll be a perticularly unlucky day for Steve Hart. It's a outlandish country, this Afriky, isn't it Mestur Ralph ? " "Outlandish in many respects," laughed Cart- leigh. "In quite a different sense to what you mean, too. Don't you read the newspapers, Ben?" "Well, no; yigh, a bit sometimes," stammered Ben. "Yo' see Mestur Ralph, it's a this road. I have no' brass to spare for peppers every day, an' as I'm a member of th' Co-op. I go to th' readin'-room sometinies of a neet, but whenever I happen to go, owd Bodle is sure to be theer. Yo' know Bodle, I reckon ? Well, he's theer, an' he does his readin' like his talkin', yo' know, follows every line o' th' print wi' his finger an' speaks th' words out loud, or in a sort of whisper-talkin', an'—an'---I canno' stand it, an' I go to th' ale- house i'stead of improvin' my mind wi' readin'. I'll bet owd Bodle's driven many another man to drink wi' you trick of his."

"You were talking of South Africa being an out- landish place," resumed Cartleigh. "Well if you'd read the papers lately you would have noticed that in Johannesburg, South Africa, there are men called Outlanders."

"Oh, yigh. I've heard of 'em," interrupted Ben. "I read about 'em when I were at schoo'. They're thoose savage, cannibal chaps 'at eat our missionaries up, are no' they. Yigh, I know. 'An' thoose are Outlanders, eh? By gow ! If. Steve Hart drops into their hands, an' finally into their mouths, it'll be a misfortin' for him, an' no mistake. Egow ! they are a' outlandish crowd."

-" No, yo li are quite mistaken, Ben," said Cartleigh, when he could manage to speak, "these Outlanders are not the man-eating savages you imagine them to be. Many of them are Englishmen, like you or I. They are merely called , Outlanders or Tritlanders by the Dutchmen of South Africa. An Outlander is a man from the out-lands, from other countries."
"Oh, I see; they're gradely, dacent, civilised s" people?" t o."
"Then Steve will be a' Outlander when he gets to that outlandish country?" "He will. Steve, the Outlander,' will be quite an appropriate name for him." _ _

Tliere was a self-satisfied sneer on the young man's face as he uttered the words, but it was not noted by burly Ben, who went back to his work, laughing at the "young mestur's wit." Ralph Cartleigh was much amused with the idea of this young fellow Hart going out fortune-hunting in far-off Africa.

"A raw, callow youth," he mused, "who has spent his years in a mule-gate, going out to a country to contend with men, the sharpest, the cleverest, the keenest on earth. The idea likes me well. Doubtless this young fool is going out in the belief that he will be able to shovel gold up as our colliers shovel coals. Bucketsful he will get, no doubt. What precious fools we do breed these days! Ben is right. If the greenhorn could, but see, as I see, where true wealth is, he wouldn't leave it behind him in my father's weaving-shed. Ha Iha All things ai-e progressing beautifully for me! A short time ago I had anticipated trouble with this fortune-hunter, but now, thanks to his greed and cupidity, he leaves me in complete possession of the field. Once let him get aboard his lugger and the girl is mine, the fortune is mine, his miss-fortune as Ben facetiously, puts it. Egad I played the trump card last week when I told Brannan not to let Hart have that pair of mules. Hart has enough mules in himself. He is a perfect jackass, and the fun of it is he doesn't know it. He had an ambition to become a minder, a full- ,blown spinner. I'll be the minder now—the other sort; I'll mind her carefully while he's away." , So pleased with himself was Ralph Cartleigh,! that he left business and office work behind for a time, and went to an adjacent public-house where he drank success to "Steve, the Outlander." "A safe, a verysafe and pleasant voyage may he have next week!" he chuckled.
(To be continued.)

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

In regard to millinery I may observe that there seems to be a return to the flimsy and garish style of a season or two back, from which I thought we had escaped. This shows chiefly amongst the toques, composed mainly of tulle, or mousseline— not the most comfortable looking materials for north-east winds, sleet, rain, and other little pleasantries peculiar to the English spring of prosy fact—which are a mass of aggressive feathers, flowers, buckles, and etcetras of opposing hues and wild outline. The hats are happily less on the lines of the toques, which one must hope will temper their present mood and become less aggressive as the semon advances. The new straws have chenille interwoven or planted; some have threads of gold and silver running through.

Present wear show the long and the short varieties of coat. One worn is cloth of a warm, fawn shade, almost verging on tan, but with a good dash of mouse-colour in it. The revers are made of open-worked cloth, bordered with beaver fur, the high collar and cuffs matching this trim- ming. The coat is made long enough' to rest on the ground, but in this item it need not be imi- tated when meant for wear in walking. Who coats for driving should be rather long, so that they may afford some protection to the ankles. I have seen a bolero jacket fastening on the left shoulder with a large button in steel and oxydised silver. The wide collar was bordered with ermine.

I have recently seen some dresses designed for outdoor wear in the spring. For the most part walking gowns give a cloth surtout, with flounce, revers and collars of zibeline; a black band of velvet is brought from the back of the shoulders and fmiqhed off with bows in front. Another gown is of mauve cloth.

The colour of the moment for outdoor garments, including dresses, coats, and hats, is undoubtedly khaki. It is certainly not particularly becoming, especially to women with light brown or flaxer hair and pale or sallow complexions, but it doe! not show mud and dirt, and if its drabness h judiciously alleviated with a more decided tint, the first-named drawback is minimised. One oi the smartest of recently-seen khaki gowns is oi face cloth, and has a deep pointed tunic falling over a kilted flounce of rich blue silk. The bodice is made with_ a very small bolero of the cloth, cut round at the neck. Green goes extremely well with khaki, although it is less kind to the com- plexion of the wearer than crimson or blue, while a woman with a bright colour may venture on a per- fectly plain tailor-made gown of khaki cloth, with a simple stitched skirt and a little coat-bodice fastened with gilt military buttons and faced with khaki velvet.

Hair-dressing is not particularly elaborate at present, but it must be very carefully done—if it is to be really fashionable, that it to say. It is no longer good style to wear the hair over the ears, nor is it so enormously puffed out over wire rouleaux as was the case a few months ago, but it is still waved in large undulations and combed up loosely (over a smailcircitiar pad if the tresses are not over abundant) to the very top of the head, where it is gathered into a small, rather high- standing coil. The front hair is waved and rolled loosely back and twisted with the rest, only a very few light curls being allowed to rest either in the exact centre of the forehead or on the temples. The fringe covering the whole of the forehead is happily quite aching of the past. Very dainty little head-dresses are being worn with evening dress. A chaplet of leaves arranged round the coiffure just above the forehead curls is a novelty, but one which suits only a few faces, and the stigrettes placed close to and nearly in front of the coil at the top are more generally becoming than jnonster butterflies in cut jet; tufts of feathers rising from ribbon bows or paste clasps, and rosettes of lace or baby-ribbon which conceal the stems of a pair of rose-buds or a knot of violets, are all popu- lar, and if well arranged look extremely smart and stylish. .
Your loving JENNIE.

Princess Margaret of Connaught is to make her first appearance at the Drawing Booms this season. She has recently entered upon her nineteenth year, and the fact reminds us that there will soon be very few of the Queen's grandchildren remaining in their teens. Apart from the young B,,ttenberg family, the youngest among them is Victoria Patricia of Connaught, who is four years youneer than her sister, and three years junior to Princess Alice of Albany. Princess Margaret of Con- naught scarcely looks her age, and in appearance no one would think there are four years between the sisters. Bugler Dunn, of the Dublin Fes hers who was pre- sented the other day to the Queen at o:.horne, is unques- tionably the boy of the hour. Not only has the Army good case to be proud of him, buthe must be the envy of every boy in the country. The lad has been in three engagements. and was wounded in the battle of Colenso in the first attempt to cross the Tugela. Dunn rushed forward with the firing line, in spite of the endeavours, of some of the soldiers to keep him back, and he fell wounded in the arm and chest. When rescued, his bugle was missing, and the loss has been a great grief to him. The Queen however, presented him with a handsome new bugle, which will he highly prized, and no doubt more than recompense him for the loss. The little bugler has only recently been discharged from Netley Hospital, anti when Princess Christian asked him what he would like the Queen to do for him when he got well, be said he hoped Her Majesty would send him back again to the front. Like so many of the bugler and drummer boys of the Army, Dunn has spent his whole life with the colours, and the regiment of which his father is Sergeant, and who is also on active dervice in South Africa. Lis not likely that Dann will be sent back, but it is to be hoped that be will not be spoilt by all the lionising and the petting, of which he is just now the object. The women of the Transvaal and the Free State, we are told, are clamouring for arms, wherewith to fight beside their husbands and brothers, and, on our side,a woman correspondent writes to the papers to suggest the formation of a " Women's Volunteer Rifle Force," to help in the defence of the country. She anticipates that her proposal will be received with a general fusilade of satire and ridicule, but hopes nevertheless, that this will not deter some organiser coming forward to take the scheme in hand. There ought to be, she says,a rifle range in every village, and she cannot see why there should not be markswomen as well as marksmen. In South Africa there is not a family of the old Voer- trekking stock, but what has its traditions of valour and desperate courage on the pan of the women, as well as of its men, and, in this coentry, there are, we know, many women who are experts in handling the gun. These however, are- the exceptions, and when the " Women's Rifle Force "was out at practice with ball cartridge, most people would desire to leave the neigh- bourhood. Considering that the modern weapon may be fatal at any distance up to two miles, tbe only safe place would be the cellar, when firing was on, and with every village busy at the musketry bu9ines,, we should no doubt soon have an efficient system for thinning out the superfluous population. The women of Canada have a more practical scheme in hand than that of the individual who suggests that they should take to firearms and fighting. This is a movement entitled " The daughters of the Empire," which has been inaugurated at Montreal, to totter the bond of union between the Homeland and the Colonies, to encourage Imperial patriotism, and to help forward those forces which seem at last to be sweeping on to- wards a Federated Empire. It is a movement which everyone in this country would wish to encourage. No small share of the sorrow, due to the war, falls upon the women, and in Canada and Australia they have just as freely parted with their husbands and brothers,as is the case in this country. One of the most striking features of the war has been the surpassing loyalty and enthu- siasm to which it has given rise in Canada.Australia,and other Colonies, and, in every practical form, there ought to be a hearty response in this country to the patriotic action of the women of Canada.

The attraction at Earls Court (London), this summer, will be the" International Women's Exhibition "which is to be opened in May. The display will be entirely devoted to things concerning our sex, both in work, and play, and the management has succeeded in obtaining the names and assistance of many well-known women in the fashionable world. No fewer than nine or ten duchesses figure upon the honorary and executive com- mittee. It would scarcely be possible to give all the names YAW) include the Duchess of York, Lady Roths- child, the Baroness Burdett-Coutts, Lady Audrey Buller. the Countess of Aberdeen, the Countess of Warwick, and many other women of note, not only in this country but the Colonies and Europe generally. The Exhibition will be divided into sections, showing theeprogress of women in the fine arts, in industrial and doutestic work, in edocation and so an. There is te be a Hospital Section and the Industrial Section will make a special feature of cottage and other women's indus- tries. Among other displays there will be one devoted to House Decoration, illustrating the latest improve- ments for the lyauty and comfort of the home. Another will be for women's dress, fashions, etc., ard the Nur- sery Section will, of course, specially refer to the health, dress, food, and education of children. Altogether the Exhibition promises to be one of exceptional interest and nsefulness. .

During the at week or RO many up to date women have teen wearing a band of black tulle round the throat, studded with diamonds or other precious stones to match those worn on the corsage, and in the hair. Such a state of affairs was not unexpected. The Princess of Wales recently appeared with her neck adorned in this particular manner, it was therefore a foregone conclu- sion that the idea would be extensively copied Un- doubtedly it is a most becoming mode, and it promises to remain with us during the spring and Early summer months.

The new tulle used this season is delightfully strong and yet fine and filmy as ever. It is almost proof again& tearing and however crumpled, a warm iron will trans form itinto new again. Black tulle frocks are in great request for evening wear just now, the fabric lending itself se. well to the transparent billowy messes deemEd correct, High sleeveless evening bodices have lately made their appearance. It has been said, and .probably there is much of truth in the statement, that these garments have been specially invented for those women posseceed of pretty arms, and unduly developed salt cellars." However this may be. they are undoubtedly ugly and and unbecoming to a degree. A transparent sleeve and transparent yoke are much more desirable from every point of view.
" MADGE."

div.head: STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
div.p: STEVE, THE OUTLANDER.
By ARTHUR LAYCOCK, Author of "The Young Gaffer," "Seaside Sketches," "Lancashire Sketches," &c.

div.head: CHAPTER L
div.p: CHAPTER L

In the gloaming of a fair June evening a youth and maiden strolled aimlessly along the tow-path of a canal which skirts the southern fringe of Dalesworth, a small manufacturing town situate midway between Oldham and Manchester. In appearance the couple were much like other couples who strolled about. They were of the factory operative class. The girl neatly, almost smartly, attired, was somewhat pale of feature, but, withal, her face was fair to look upon. Her figure was well-rounded and shapely, and seen to advantage in her easy, graceful carriage. From time to time she glanced furtively at her companion, who, with hands behind his back and dogged, defiant expression on his face, walked silently beside her. He was a well-set, sturdy young fellow, of better physique than the average mill hand. Save for his pale cast of feature the close confinement of the factory seemed to have had no injurious effect upon him. As they came to a less frequented part of the tow-path he looked up at the girl, and a warm tinge of colour mounted to his cheeks as he met her inquiring gaze. "Now tell me, Steve," she said, "tell me what it is that is troubling you. • What has gone wrong this time ? "

"Oh, ,everything has gone wrong," he answered, hastily. "Everything does go wrong with me lately." "Everything, Steve? Have I-" "No, no," he replied, quickly. "No, Ella, it isn't you. I forget what I say. lam bothered. You, thank goodness, have not gone wrong. It's my work. Curse the work! Curse the factories and those that invented 'em ! "

"0 Steve, why do you say that? What should we do without the factories? What could I do? Why, mother and I would have to starve if I couldn't get work at weaving." "You're not far removed from starvation as it is, more's the pity. And look at me. I've been a little piecer for years. I'm now a big piecer and have been for two years, with a wage of seventeen shillings a week. Seventeen shillings a week for a full-grown man! What is it? Barely enough for me to keep going on after paying for granny's keep. What chance is there for me to save anything? What chance for us to get married ? " "But you're sure to get a pair of wheels before long. It's your turn next." "It has been 'my turn next' before," the young fellow replied, bitterly. "You know that I ought to have had a pair of wheels three months since, but Jackson was placed before me. I shall never get a pair of mules at Cartleighs', that's certain." "Why, what makes you say that, Steve ? " "I'll tell you in a minute. They now turned aside down a by-path leading to a little secluded dough in the lgedlock Vale. "I shall never get a pair of mules while young Cartleigh is about the place. I tell you, Ella, he hates me. It was he who told Brannan to let Jackson have the mules in preference to me." "0 Steve!" said the girl, in a tone of remon- strance. "I don't think he would do that."
"But I know, Ella, he did do that. Didn't Brannan himself tell me ? "
"Well, I don't see why he should be prejudiced against you. Mr. Ralph is always very nice to me." •
Stephen Hart shot a swift, suspicious glance at his companion, and she drooped her eyes under his keen gaze. "I mean—l mean he is nice with all the girls," she stammered.

"Of course he is, the scamp! That's why I distrust him. Nice with all the girls, eh, and especially with you? Why isn't he nice with all the men, or why isn't he fair with them, at any rate? I tell you, Ella, I don't like Ralph Cartleigh." "Well," said the girl, with spirit, "1 think you are very hard on him, Stephen Hart. I've never seen anything wrong about him, and I don't think Brannan wan telling the t,ruth about that affair of Jacison's. "

"Oh, well," said the young man, halting abruptly, "if you don't believe Brannat, don't believe me." His face flashed anger as he con- tinued more vehemently. "But, above all, do believe in that immaculate young Cartleigh. You seem to have a great liking for him, but "—with bitter sarcasm— 'I suppose you are like the rest." "Like the rest? What do you mean? Don't be silly, Steve. If I thought that you really meant anything by such remarks I wouldn't speak to you again." Then, in a changed manner, she tossed her head roguishly and beckoned to him. "Now, come along, and forget all about it." She slipped her arm through his and they proceeded on their way. "You are troubled, Steve, and don't think of what you say." "I know what I say, Ella," he rejoined, less bitterly, for he was yielding to her soothing influence. "I say bitter things, but if you knew all that Ido you would understand. But we'll not quarrel, my- girl. Mind, though, Ella, if things turn out bad this next week, as I expect they will, I shall clear out." "Oh!" laughed the, girl, gaily. "Clear out, will you? Clear away from me, will you? I should like to know how you would get along with- out me, Sir Rebel. Try for a second," and with a playful push she started him down the slope. She caught him up in a moment. . "Now,, how would you manage, do you thi.nk ? "

"I should get on badly without you, Ella," he answered, seriously, not heeding her joking manner. "You know what you are to me. I should not have stuck at the mill as I have but for your close companionship.. I wanted to be near you. But I tell you, Ella, if I don't get the pair of wheels that Sayers is leaving next week I shall go abroad." "Go abroad ? " the girl repeated, in surprise. "Yes, I shall go abroad, Ella. There's more chance of making a fortune in South Africa than there is in a Dalesworth cotton mill, even with a pair of wheels. I shall for a time lose my best fortune in you, Ella, but it is for you that I desire to win the other fovtune."

"0 Steve!" cried the girl, in dismay, now realising that he was in earnest. "You mustn't talk of such a thing as going away from here. What should Ido without you? Oh, you mustn't think of such —a thing."' They had now arrived at Daisy Nook, the favoured rendezvous of the lads and lasses for miles around. Here, on an open-air dancing platform, scores of young folks were tripping the light fantastic toe to the strains of a brass band which was playing a rollicking polka. Ella Rayburn and Stephen Hart joined the merry, whirling throng, and one of the twain had soon wholly dismissed from thought the conversation which had recently passed between them.

Ella Rayburn was in the hey-day of her woman- hood, at that period of her life when she permitted nothing to lie heavily on her senses. She thought of dress, she thought of display, she thought of danc- ing, of holidays, and other pleasant things; she thought of Steve—a little, she thought of herself much. But of matters disconcerting and unpleasant she thought not at all. She liked the gay and sunny side of life, the shadow she left for others. Steve was in the shadow now; well, he would come out of it. No need for her to trouble. Life was jolly; she was pretty; Steve was a devoted lover; all was well. The sun shone for her, and that was sufficient. A selfish, thoughtless, giddy, whimsical girl. Such was Ella Rayburn. The factory master's son, Ralph Cartleigh, had singled her out for special notice from amongst the weavers at Fern- leigh Mill. This pleased the girl mightily. It was a high tribute to her personal charms. Besides, it made the other girls jealous, and that was gratify- ing to Ella. But whilst dearly appreciating the attentions of young Cartleigh, she had no intention of giving him a higher place in her/affections than her avowed lover. Steve would some day rise to a good position in life, of that she was assured; poor judge of human character though she was, she could yet perceive that he possessed grit, perseverance, determination—qualities which would secure for him success in his undertakings, sooner or later.

Steve was a pleasing young fellow, too, good- looking, and normally good4emoered. Her girl companions envied her luck in securing him. He was considered to be "a good catch," by these dis- criminating young ladies. All was well with Ella; the cloud which over- shadowed her lover would pass way. Therefore she danced light-heartedly; infecting her companion with her ac,y'aoirits. As they returned homeward

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.

The week-end, with its gla,m,our • and glory, .had passed into the realm of bygones. As the gay sun rose above the housetops and swiftly dispersed the early morning mists, the clatter of clogs made bustling sound in the streets of Dalesworth* as the factory operatives hurried to their work. .The "buzzers (steam whistles) were droning sonorously all over the district, warning the workpeople that six o'clock was nigh.

At Fernleigh Mill a constant stream of men, women, and children flowed through the big lodge gates. Smart spinners in peaked caps and clean white jackets and moleskin breeches; weaver lasses in hats, van-coloured shawls and skirts of dark material; little piecers, tricky, talkative youngsters, with wealth of corduroy about them, and tenters, pale little lasses in garb part girlish, part womanish. An active, bright, alert, bustling, jostling throng all swarming into the mighty gate- jaws, to be swallowed up in a moment and be passed into every part of the huge• factory. Foremost in the crowd was Stephen Hart, eager and expectant. He hurried towards the spinning-room, and at the entrance met the spinners' manager, Brannan. "Well, am I a minder this morning ? " Steve asked, as he advanced. "No, lad, tha'rt not," said Brannan, speaking in the vernacular as was his want. "Tha'rt nobbut big piecer yet, Steve, I'm sorry to say. Better luck next time."

A look of keen disappointment flitted across the young man's face, but b.is fixed resolution buoyed him up. "There'll be no next time' for me, Brannan. I'll be a big piecer no more after this week. There's .no chance of advance:Anent for me.at this place, seemingly, so I'll leave it." "Just al tha likes, Stve ; just as tha likes," said Brannan, —turning into the spinning-room. "If tha'rt for goin' at th' week-end, go give 'em thy notice at th' office now."

Steve went off as directed and returned a few minutes later to labour at the task which was now more wearying than ever. In this spinning-room he had toiled strenuously and well, going through the various stages as little piecer, big piecer, and joiner-minder, with ever the inspiriting-hope that some day, in his due turn, he would be advanced to a minder's position, one of the best-paid positions in the factory. Now his hopes wore dashed to the ground. To-day, as three months ago, he saw others secure the coveted pair, of wheels. Well, thank goodness, he saw the end of it now I He yearned for the breakfast half-hour, that he might tell his sweetheart how soon his factory work would end. At last the clang and rattle of machinery ceased. Quickly the toilers seized hats, caps, and shawls, and with breakfast cans and food dined out in the open air this fair summer's morn.

, Ella and Steve met in the yard, and the young man at once broke into violent speech. "I told you how it would turn out, Ella. Someone else has been appointed to take charge of the pair of mules I ought to have had. Everyone in the place considers that I have been treated shabbily. Brannan himself admits it. That joung Cartleigh is to blame for this. I know ke is. He came sneaking, round ivatching me in the mule-gate just after I'd been in the office to tell them I was leav- ing at the week-end. The young sneak will take a special delight in my disappointment. Let hint come near enough again; I'll give him something that wont give him delight." "It is a downright shame, Steve, that you have been treated so unfairly," said the girl ; "but never mind, it can't be helped now. Perhaps you can get in somewhere else." "Never!" he replied, emphatically. "If I went anywhere else I should have to work for years as a big piecer as I have done here, wait my turn, then probably be treated like this again. No; I have done with factory work after this week."

He explained more fully his plans for the future. He would embark for South Africa on Thursday of the following week. In the meantime he would make arrangements for Granny Hart, his sole living relation, to be attended to in his absence. In the new country, where a man would have plenty of scope, he would labour hard and prosper greatly. Of that he had not the slightest doubt. Henceforward his past life of monotonous drudgery would be forgotten. Ella alone would be remembered, and the thought of her would ever inspire him in his new sphere.

"-But what will you do? What will you work at ? " Ella asked. "There are no factories in South Africa, are there ? " "No, thank goodness, there are not," he answered. "I'm not quite sure yet what I shall work at; gold-digging, I hope. Something good is sure to turn up. Anyhow, I reckon I shall stand as good a chance as the other fellows who go out, and if I'm not actually getting the gold I shall perhaps be rubbing against the fellows who are getting it, and in that case some of it is certain to stick on me."

He was very sanguine and had the great expecta- tions which all young emigrants cherish. Within the course of a few days the news spread throughout the factory that Stephen Hart was going abroad on the following week. Gossip travels quickly in a cotton mill, particu- larly in the weaving-shed, where oral language is useless owing to the deafening rattle of machinery, but where sign-language is all-sufficient, and is in constant use by the female operatives. From the weaving-shed to the spinning-room, from thence to the warehouse, and finally to the office, the news spread. Young Mr. Cartleigh received the information from Ben Potter, the burly warehouseman. "I've Ikard, Mestur Cartleigh," said Ben, as he waddled into the private office on Tuesday forenoon, "I've heard 'at Steve Hart is for goin' to Afriky, next week."

"Is that so, Ben ? " said'the young man, smiling grimly, as he quietly closed the door. "Is he going to seek for a fortune, think you, Ben? " "For a miss-fortune, I think, Mestur Ralph," replied the jocular fellow, "for there's a woman concerned in th' business, yo' mun know, an' th' miss fortune he'll make will be in leavin' that Miss behind. He may miss this feminine fortune awtogether if he goes seekin' for t'other." "To which particular miss are you referring, Ben? " asked young Cartleigh. He knew who would be named, but wished to glean as much .news as possible from the cossininEr warehouseman.

div.head: NORTHERN CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. --- Smart Performance by Sankey Harriers.
div.p: NORTHERN CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. --- Smart Performance by Sankey Harriers.

The day opened with fine bright weather and several special .:rains arrived in R ,thirham about noon bring- ing numerous supporters of the various teams that were competing to witness the race. The clubs expected to win honours wore Bolton, Broughton, and Gateshead, whilst Sankey were fancied to run well no, although they were being without the services of Jack Riley, a prominent runner, who was debarred from assisting his club. he having won a medal in the senior race 3 years ago. During the week, J Wilding, one of the tesm that was chosen, was taken ill with influenza, but a good substitute was found in E. anti°. The course was a severe one, and with the heavy thaw in the latter part ef the week made the going exceedingly he vv. A lap of about a mile and three quarters had been mapped out, and consistrd of three ploughed fields, with hurdles 2tt. flin. high interspersed throughout the circuit. The num- ber of clubs competing was 17, allowing 9 from each to run, nicking 153 runners, who were started at 3 45, at a fast pace. Ezard, of Bolton Primrose Harriers, was leading in the first circuit, but after, Hughes.Gateshead took the lead and ultimately won easily by 320 yards in 43 minutes 44 srcends. div.head: TEE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: TEE FREE CHURCHES.

"ILK.," of the Methodist Recorder (the Rev. 2Fehemiah Curnock, the editor) contributes an interesting article to the March Free Church Chronicle on the Rev. C. H. Kelly, the new Pre- sident of the National Free Church Council. Mr. Kelly did great service to his denomination and to all the Free Churches by his valiant and successful fight for the right of Nonconformist soldiers to attend their own place of worship. In 1859 he was appointed to work among the soldiers at Aldershot. Says Mr. Curnock : "His preachitg attracted men in crowds. I have heard it said in Aldershot that if room could have been found, the whole town would have flocked to his ministry. The parade services in the iron church had to be doubled. A crack regiment in the cavalry barracks, with the colonel at their head, used to march in a body to the iron church." Mr. Kelly has the rare and subtle gift of personal magnetism. From general officers, through all ranks, down to the humblest recruit, he charmed men or overawed them. He has preached in more than 600 different churches, and has never had to break an engagement through ill-health. His services to the Free Church Federation movement have been beyond price, and he has fully won the honour which he now bears.

div.head: DR. PARKER AND THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: DR. PARKER AND THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Dr. Parker,evidently does not think much ot our legislators at Westminster. He has been giving his views on the debate on the Address. He applies the following adjectives to it: Mean, paltry, worthless, atheistic, inhuman, contemptible, disastrous. "The debate," he says," made me sore and sick at heart." Mr. Balfour asked, in the course of his speech, "To whom are the Boers looking for support ?" and Mr. "Tim" Healy replied, "God." This one word, says Dr. Parker, was the greatest speech,of the debate, and Mr. Healy is "one of the brightest intellects of the century." This is all very interesting,. but Dr. Parker does not say that Mr. Healy was the only Christian man in the House of Commons, nor even that he was the best Christian there. However, Mr. Healy's speech of one word did Dr. Parker's heart good, "poor, old, withered, disappointed heart."

div.head: FREE CHURCH GIRLS' GUILD.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCH GIRLS' GUILD.

The final scheme of this Guild, which will aim at doing for the young women of the Free Churches what the Girls' Friendly Society does for the young women of the Anglican Church, has been approved by the General Committee of the National Free Church Council, and will be presented to the delegates at Sheffield by Mrs. George Cadbury, who has taken a special interest in the question.. There is to be a Central Bureau at London in connection with the National Council, and this bureau will be in communication with a certain special com- mittee of every local Council. The object is to band together the girls of the Free Churches, and to secure that they shall find friends wherever they go. Arrangements will be made for co-operation with. kindred existing Societies, such as the Y.W.C.A.., Dr. Stephenson's Gies Taielpful Society, and other bodies. Such Free Church organisation on a large &Twat wits impossible until the Free Church Council wane into existence.
MACLAREN OF MANCHESTER."

Dr. Maclaren, the famous Baptist preachsr of Manchester, has just completed his seventy- fourth year. Though he has had two sore bereavements of late, he has not allowed his personal sorrow to interfere in any way with his ministerial work. One who listened to him the other Sunday, and who has "sat under" him often, said that he had never preached with greater power. Dr. Maclaren is very con- servative in some things, he will never oven hear of announcing beforehand tze subjects or even the texts of his sermons. We trust that some years of fruitful work in Manchester are still before him.

div.head: AN UNWISE CURATE.
div.p: AN UNWISE CURATE.

The enfant terrible of the Anglican Church is the young curate whose sectarian zeal is with- out good manners or knowledge. For instance, a young man at Padstow, whose remarks are receiving more attention than they deserve, in- formed the parishioners that "Dissent is the direct outcome of tares sown by the devil." We may be perfectly certain that the wisest and noblest men in the State Church are much annoyed and shocked by an utterance of this sort. It makes the Anglican Communion ridiculous, and damages Christianity; for, as Dr. Fairbairn has wisely said, no form of Christianity can be served by any other form being made ridiculous. The Padstow curate's unwisdom is harmful to Nonconformity only as it is harmful to the general interests of Chris- tianity.
THE ORIGIN OF BAPTISTS.-A NEW VERSION..

How pitiful and disastrous it is that there should be so many duplicates of the Padstow curate! A certain Anglican localised maga- zine, in an article on ." The True Church," informs us that the story of the origin of the Baptists is "one of the darkest in history, branded as it is with the wildest fanaticism and crime." And yet we spend many millions a year—not too many certainly—on education! The writer informs us that John Calvin, " in- vented" Presbyterianism in 1541, and we are told that it is everyone's duty to avoid "mere human and voluntary associations of people Who have agreed to unite together in professing Certain Christian doctrines, and to style them- selves Christian Church.— These "human and voluntary associations" to be avoided are Congregational, Baptist, Presbyterian and Methodist Churches throughout the English- speaking world, possessing over seventeen million communicants !

div.head: BERRY MEMORIAL SCHOLARSHIP.
div.p: BERRY MEMORIAL SCHOLARSHIP.

We cordially wish success to the movement for the institution of a Berry Memorial Scholarship at Mansfield College, the competi- tion for which will be open to all the Free Churches of the country. There is at present no such scholarship at Mansfield, and Dr. Fairbairn says well that when it is founded, ig it could bear no name so fitly as that of Dr. Berry, who did so much for the Federation • ovement."

div.head: CHEERFUL FOLK.
div.p: CHEERFUL FOLK.

By Cheerful Folk Ido not moan people who are always laughing. Mr. Spurgeon says :—" The man who is always laughing is a fool." Big doses of giggleism do not make for cheerfulness. Some people are so much in the habit of complaining they've got to like it, and are only happy when they're miserable. We're sure of it. We heard of a man living at Bradford who had a habit of looking miserable, and always walking with his head down and eyes fixed on thc pavement. The people in the town say that when he first \ came to live there many years ago he lost a bhreepenny-bit, kad had bean looking for it ever since. Cheerful people are always thankful people. Some people metsure a man's religion bY the length of his face. Away with such cant. A man's religion should be judged by the breadth of his face. Let us try to be worthy of the poet's eulogy—"A man he seemed of cheerful yesterdays, and confident to-morrows." div.head: DEATH OF MR. T. GLAZE BROOK RYLANDS.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. T. GLAZE BROOK RYLANDS.

It is with the deepest regret that we record the death of Mr. Thomas Glazehrook Rylands one of the directors of the firm of Messrs. Rylands Bros. Li mited,wire manuf acturers,C hurch-st , who passed away at his residence at Thelwall on Thursday last week.lnlthe public affairs of Warrington the name of Rylands has been long and honourably associated, and the present position of the town is to some extent due to the labours of the distinguished metabers of this family. Latterly, advancing age had some what retarded Mr.T.G. Rylands'usefulness,and prevented him from taking any part in local Noe' none. He was therefore little known bY the rising generation. The deceased gentleman was a brother of the late Mr. Peter Rylands, formerly member of Parliament for Warringtoe and Burnley. and was the last of the three brothers, He was the oldest borough magistrate but had not been able to take his seat on the Bench for sixteen years, and prior to that time his attendance was very intermittent.

r. Rylands's connection with the Warrington Corporation commenced in March, 1851, when be was elected an auditor of the borough. In the fa" lowing year he was. returned a councillor and 10 February 1854, the Council honoured him by elect bag him an alderman. Pour years later he was appointed chief magistrate of the Borough and discharged the onerous duties during 1858 and 1859. Be was re-elected an alderman in the last named year and again in 1865. ShortlY afterwards he retired from municipal work and his interest in public affairs appre— ciably diminished. Like ilia brothers be WO a Liberal in politics. but he did not play so pro- minent a part. During the last twenty years be has rarely been seer in the town acting in an/ public capacity. He was formerly President of the Warringto.o Literary and Philosophical Society and Vice-Presi— dent of the Liverpool Historic Society, and had con- tributed a large number of papers to bath .ocietieS• He was also a member of the Society of Antiquaries, the Linemus Society, the Geological Society, the Royal Geographical Society,and the Royal Astrono- mical Sof Ity.Hetook a deep interest in a wide range' ot scientific subjects and his contributions to litera- ture are to be found in the Warrington Reference Library. A list of them will give some idea of tbe subjects which interested the deceased gentleman. In 1843 he published a pamphlet entitled "An in- quiry into tobacco smoke." A little later at the lectures held in connection with the Warrington Mechanics Institute Mr. Rylands contributed 6 paper on the "Moon" which was reprinted. In 185 t he wrote a paper on "Stones and Crystals"; in 187 r one on " Ptolemy's Geography of the Coast ;" 1879," Map history of the Coast from the Dee Or the Duddon;" and in 1880," Winwick and Culcheth! These four papers were read before the Liverpool Historic Society.. In 1893 he published an importaJi,',. work entitled "Geography of Ptolemy illustrated: Atone time Mr. Rylands had an observatory at his house, which he afterwards offered to the Warring- ton Corporation, but as they were unable to pro- vide accommodation for it the offer was made to the Liverpool University who accepted it. 10: Rylands was a stEdent of botany and geology Ana roade extensive collections and researches.

He leaves two sone and an unmarried daughter. His sons are Mr. Paul nylon(ls and _Mr. Hera Rylands both of whom are barristers. At Mr. Ryland's request his remains were ere' mated at the Manchester Crematorium 011 (Saturday). The ceremony was of a strictlY private character. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE. At the conclusion e,f the ordinary business at tbe Warrington Police Court, on Friday morning, The MAYOR said he should like to take tbf!. opportunity of saying on behalf of himself and 131! colleagues on the Bench, how much they regretted to hear of the death of the oldest borough magis' trate—Mr. Rylands. Although it was runny yesr3 since beset on the Bench, at one time he took 110 active interest in matters connected with the administration of the law. As a member of the Cors poration and an ex-Mayor he had done a very goo° work. He was asseciated with a family havrnit, an illustrious connection with everything coneerne° in the municipal adMinistration ot the town. Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the solicitors pre' tising at the court expressed similar sentiments. IP said that altllough Mr Ry lands as a magiArate we° hardly within their recollection,he not having sat for 16 yeare,tbey had always beard of him as an impar: tie!, fair, and really Rood magistrate. He endorse' the remarks of the Mayor.

div.head: KICKING OUTRAGE AT WARRINGTON. Trial of W;I--h at Liverpool.
div.p: THE KICKING OUTRAGE AT WARRINGTON. Trial of W;I--h at Liverpool.
Five Years Penal Servitude.

In the Crown Court at Liverpiol Astzs on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Grantham, Thomas Walsh, aged 401 an ironwork a-. was indicted for haying Gn January 4,at the borough of Warrington, feloniously, wilfully, and of his malica aforethought killed and murdered 0119 Joseph Swift. Mr. Tobin and Mr. Maxwell (instructed by Mr. J. Lyon Wnittle, t)svn clerk of Warrington) prosecuted on behalf of the Crown,and Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington) ctifeuded. Toe prisoner pleaded net guilty to the indictment as read by the clerk of arraigns (Sir Herbert Stephen). Counsel's Opening Statement.

Mr. Tobin, in opening the ca—se, said that, serious as the facts were, he hoped that, under his lordship's direction, the jury would be able to find a lesser verdict than that ot wilful murder. The deceased and the prisoner were both engaged at Messrs Pearson and Knowles's iron works, Warrington. Tney did not know each other,but their wives were acquainted. On January 3 the wives met in the town and went to a public-house, and afterwards to Swift's house, where in company with Swift, they had some liquor. After a time a quarrel arose, and Mr and Mrs Swift put out Mrs Wallin, who proceeded to break the windows. While she was being put out. Mrs Walsla's shawl fell off, and she wont away without it. At eight o'clock next morning prisoner and his wife arrived at the back door of Swift's house, and said they had come for the shawl. The door was Opened and prisoner commenced to violently attack Swift. He hit him in the face, and Swift being the weaker man, and at any rate less able to use his fists—because prisoner was a professional pugilist, going about giving boxing exhibitions at fairs, &s.—retreated into the front room. prisoner followed and attacked him again. Swift then tried to escape upstairs, and prisoner follow- ing gave him a running kick b-tween the kegs. The prisoner was wearing the clogs produced, with wooden soles and iron ties, with which he kicked Swift from behind and between the legs. Swift went upstairs and locked the door, and the prisoner and his wife went away. Swift's wife afterwards went up to her husband, and found him in great pain from a large lump between his legs. A doctor was sent for, and Swift was removed to the Infirmary, where he died eleven days afterwards from the results of the kick. As soon as the prisoner found out what had been the result of the kick, and that it was probably going to be very serious—i 9., after the removal of Swift to the Infirmary—the p. isoner and his wife decamped, leaving their house, and tramping across the country towards Liverpool, giving false names. These circumstances, counsel commented, were indica- tions of a guilty mind as to what he had done. Why also it was so very serious was that the prisoner was quite sober (drunkenness would not, however, have excused him), and knew what he was about. He went ostensibly to rescue his wife's shawl, but he evidently went in a spirit of revenge because his wife had b.en turned out of Swift's house, and he went to a certain extent with cold blood, kecause he went straight from his work.

The Evidence. Mary Swift, widow of Joseph Swift, 2. Russell-street, Warrington, said : My husband was 57 years of age, and was a puddler. On January 3 I met prisoner's wife, between six and seven. I had known her a little pre- viously. We went into a public-house, where I treat, d her. Afterwards we went to my house, where we had a pint of beer. Half an hour afterwards my husband came in; Mrs. Walth said her husband was not working, and I treated her, but refused to send for any more. Ste made a bother and my husband pat her out She broke nine squares of glass. On the following morning, b-- tween eight and nine. while I was in bed, and my hus- band was dressing himself,we heard a knock at the back door. Mrs. Walsh shouted, "Open this door, I want my shawl !" Her shawl had fallen off while my husband was putting her out, but we did not know it. My hus- band opened the door, and both came in without speak- ing. Walsh attacked my huebend, thumping him on the face; while Mrs Walsh assaulted me, and knocked me down. My husband got into the front room, and Walsh knocked him on the sofa,and I heard my husband saying, " Don't kill me ; I never saw you before !" Pri- soner afterwards kicked him with all his might. as far as I could see. My husband went upstairs and locked the door, and prisoner followed, but failed to burst the dour open. I heard him say, "You old pig, I'll kill you." He also said," I'll go on the stand to-night ; but, on or off the stand, I'll finish him." The prisoner was sober

at the time. In cross-examination, witness denied that her husband either threatened or struck the prisaner. Witness, further cross-examined by Mr. Swift, aemit- ted that the only blows stie saw Walsh administering to, her husband were a blow with his fist in the kitohen and the kick from behind in going upstairs. Re-examined by Mr. Tobin, witness denied that her husband returned any of the blows. Thomas Hod.eett, carter said :--I lived next door to the Swifts. On the morning of the disturbance I heard Swift say, " Oh, man, don't kill me." I did not hear Walsh say, " You old pig, I'll kill you." George Mullins a youth of fourteen, said that while , going past Swift's house be heard Swift saying, " Oh, man don't kick me." He saw Mrs Walsh in Swift's yard. I Five minutes after be ,saw the prisoner and his wife going down Dallam-lane. Dr. Curtis said that on Thursday, January 4, he was called in and found Swift in bed, and found him suffer- ing from a severe injury which might have b:en caused by a kick with a clog. He susp:!cted rupture of the urethra, and there could be no doubt that that had oceurred. By Mr. Swift: He was called in to see the deceased on Thursday night. He saw him on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. His partner saw the deceased on Saturday night also. Mr. Swift: In all human probability had a simplo operation been performed in time no fatal results would have followed? If you had performed an operation on the Friday morning in all human probably the man would now have been alive? Witness : Ido not think so. Why : Because I think that on the Friday morning there was a fair amount of urine extravasated, and he certainly would have had a better chance of recovery on the Thursday than if the operation had been performed on the Friday morning. As soon as he was removed to the Infirmary on the Sunday the doctors performed the operation ?—Yes. Believing that even then the operation might have been of some use ?—Yes. If they did it on the Sunday why could you nct have done it at once ?—Because I would not perform an operation in a house of that description. I did not think it a suitable place for an operation of any kind. You could have got blankets from the workhouse ? Yes. And you had as many instruments as you wanted ? Yes, but it was the codditien of the house. Was the reason you did not do the operation that you did not know anything about it ?—No, sir. Will you swear that I)—Yes, and I think I proved that by recommending his removal to the Infirmary. My last words to him were: " Send for a cab and go the Infirmary." You did not give him an order P—No ; it was un- necessary ; they would have admitted him. And you did not send for a cab ?—No ; I cannot force a man into the Infirmary. Did you know that if he did not go into the Infirmary the consequences must be fatal ?—Yes. If an operation was not performed ?—Yes. You knew that on Friday morning ?—Yes. And you knew that if an operation was performed at once he would probably live ?—I knew that he would have a fair chance of recovery ; yes. Have you ever performed one of these operations ? yea- Since your medical student days P—Yes ; but only once. In your opinion, were the chances of recovery remote , from the first ?—Yes. I think they were. It operated on on the Thursday night he would have had a fair chance, and if the operation had taken place imme- diately after the injury was done he would have had a very good chance. In fact, every minute reduced his chame ?—Yes. And he was left from Thursday night night till Sunday morning ?—Yes. Re-examined, witness said that the Infirmary was only six or seven minutes' walk away,and he con3idered there was danger in operating in the house. The mention of an operation frightened deceased, end he said he would stop at home. The only way witness could ineuce him to go to the Infirmary was to say that he would not'come again. He considered that deceased's only chance was an eperation in the Infirmary. In reply to his lordship, witness said that he refused to go to the prisoner on Sunday morning, and again said he must go to the Infirmary. Witness did not assist in the operation. Dr. Bowden, honorary assistant surgeon at the War- rington Infirmary, described the operation performed by him and Dr. Thorpe on the deceased, at the Infirmary on Sunday, the rich. He did not consider the operation a simple one, and he considered it would have been unwise to have performed it at the deceased's house. Cross-examined by Mr. Swift: He tbeugbt after the operation that the deceased had a chance of recovery. If the operation had ben performed immediately, he would have had a very good chance. Superintendent Monaghan testified to having received the prisoner into custody from the PreEcot police on the evening of January 8. He said" How is the old man ?" Witness replied that he had not seen him. He after- wards said, "My wife told me about having 5111,3 bother, and that they would not give her her shawl. I went down with her on the Thursday morning to try and get it for her. He ordered ins out of the house and I hit him twice—once on the nose and onco on the jaw." When afterwards charged with kicking the man, the prisoner said, "I bit him three times—once on the ribs, once on the nose,and once on the jaw. I never kicked a man in my life." div.head: DU EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 23 1900. FORESTERS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLESTOWN•
div.p: DU EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 23 1900. FORESTERS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLESTOWN•

with the wilf.al murciFr of Swift and c tutioned, said, "I am innocent of thecrim.i." Witness added that pristine: and his wife live i at Daley'd cJinnam lodg,ing-noLvA, Scotland-road, Warrington. The dying depsitions of the deceased man, Joseph Swift, were then read. Poiic:e-aergeant Klott of the Prescot Pjlice, said that on th,4 afterno i oi Januar,- 8 tie nod ;ea the prisoner going down iiitrlie-gtreet, Prescot irs the direction of uiverp )01. Ile thought he answered toe description of a man wanted as W.srringon, and accordingly sent a constable to fetch him. Toe prisons: gave the name of Bernard Riley, saving ho h?.cl come from Wigan, and bad no:. been at Warrington for three months.
Tali concluded tile ca-se for the) prosecutioa. Prisoner Gives Evidence.

Thomas Walsl-., tho prisoner, elected to give evidence on his own b!half. He said that when he went along with his wife for tor shawl to the howe of the S wilts someone called from the 'wide, " Who's there ?" His wife answered, "It is Annie Walsh, I want my shawl." Swift said, with are oath, " What do you want here? Clear out of my h4usa or you will get the same as she got last night." With that Swift struck at him, but he warded.;off. the blow as also a second one. Prisoner said to him, "I have been working all night. and I don't want any bother. I have come for my wife's shawl." He walked into the front kitchen to search for the shawl among some things lying on the sofa. While he was doing so Swift struck him again, and he turned round and struck him back, and about three or four blows were exchanged between them. He afervrards took a shovel from Mrs. Swift, with which she was going to attack him. His (prisoner's) wll2 and Swift were lying on the fl or. He pulled her away from him, saying," I have had enough of trJuble and bother with you; get off home," Swift walked upstairs, Mrs. Swift folio whiz him, and his wife set out for home, but she broke off and ran upstairs after them, and said, "You old pig, I'll give you pulling my hair." He told his wife that he wanted to go home to b3d, and they both left. Mr. Rigby Swift : During the time you were in Swift's house did you kick nim ? Prisoner : Never, sir ; I never kicked man, woman, or child since I was born. I think you are a professional pugilist ?—Yes. How did you come to leave Warrington ?—I went to work at six o'clock on M3uday morning, and about eleven o'clock my wife came to the gate saying that de- tectives had been in the house, and she was afraid they wanted her on a warrant for breaking Swift's windows. She told him that if he would not go away with hr, shG would go by herself, and he casented to go. At that time he knew nothing of any further trouble regarding Swift.

The annual dinner and meeting of fhe Court Broad Out Leg, No. 595 Ancie.e: (eider of Foresters, vas h•ld at the IVeilingtou Hotel, E trlesto een, on Stt eruey. About 40 sat d ,eeta at 5 o'clock to an excellent dinner. to wn:en full justice was done. After (hailer too room was cleared, sad the suesevent proceedings were pre- sided over oy Mr. Heap, whe was supp need by the vice-chairman. Mr. B. Aeh .rott, and the secretary, Mr. J. Lettiane. As an opening ceremony the toasts of "The Qaeen and Royal Famil7 " aud ".Tne Prince and Princess of Wales and " were prop )sei and duly honoured. Mr. J. !linden Wen rendered " Tornmv Atkins " in his best style. Toe toast " rho Army and Navy and Reserve Forces" was proposed and duly honoured, and suitably responded to by Lieutenant W. Patterson. Songs were afterwards given by Mr J Huddleistoa, " Toe Girl I Left Behind Me " ; Mr F Eean, " Soldiers of the Queen"; Mr J Huddleston, " Lily or L aguna " ; encore "Second time on Earth" ; Mr F Egan "The Diver " ; encore" Let me like a Soldier felt " ;Mr W Hill, "In days of old " ; Mr John Ball, " The Light Brigade " ; Mr Randall," Mona" ; encore "The Village Blacksmith" Mr John Ball, "Two Statesmen," ; "Toe Gallant 24th" ; Mr J Randall also rendered "The Absent Minded Beggar'. and a collection in aid of the fecal fund realised 103. A selection on the " Fairy Bells" by Mr Paton was heartily applauded. The Chairmen proposed the toast of "The High Court of Foresters," and in responding Mr. Latham remarked that during the twenty years he had been secretary of the society he had received great assistance from every member. It was an Order he was proud to be associated with and ! he had great pleasure in responding to the toast pro posed by the Chairman. The Secretary afterwards read his report in which he stated that in 1880 the sick fund of the society stood at £195 and they had 175 members, this being their quinquennial year. At this period their actuary gave them only five years as a society t live. Ten years later (also a quinquennial year) their sick funds steed at £419 and tuey had 194 members. At the end of this year comes another quinquennial year and be ventured to state that they would have better re- sults than at any other period as their sick funds now stood at £9BO arid their assets were £1,155 all of which were safely invested. They had pane 279 m •mbers £229 for sick funds whereas in 1892 they paid £lO more but this Was the year woen influenza was prevalent. Their expenses were 3i in tee £, and if they compared this with the rates of the Boards of Guardians and the benefits paid, the expense in the £ was 2s. The report was thought very satisfactory, and thanks were tendered to the Secretary for it. Mr. J• Huddleston afterwards sang" All for the sake of Finnigan," after which a very enjoyable evening was brought to a close by the customary vets of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: Speeches By Counsel.
div.p: Speeches By Counsel.

Mr. Tobin said he regretted the attack which had been made on Dr. Curtis, who did his best for the de- ceased, and advised him that an operation should 1 take place. Dr. Bowden agreed that it would have been dangerous to life to perform the operation in the man's house, and Dr. Curtis urged him to go to the Infirmary. He told him he would not attend him any more. What more could he have (Imo ? He could not drag the man to the hospital. He regretted the attack on Dr. Curtis, although there was no doubt that if the operation had been performed earlier the man's life might have been saved. That was a material element in considering what punishment should be inflicted on the prisoner. Did the prisoner kick the deceased, and did that kick result in his death? The defence was that the prisoner's wife kicked him, but they bad to seek for a reason for that. He asked the jury to find a verdict of guilty against the prisoner. Mr. Switt then addressed the Court for the defence, contending that if all the evidence against the prisoner was true his offence ameueted only to manslaughter, all the essenti7is, all tele ingredients of wilful murder being absent. Further than that he asked the jury to say that It was not prered beyond a doubt that it was the prisoner that ieflictei the injury wirich had resulted in neath. The, fact teat the prisoner was trained in the use of his hands showed the improbability of his having used his feet ; and it was more likely that the kick was administered by a woman while the deceesed was on the ground. His Lordship, in summing up, said it was clear that the prisoner had no malice beforehand towards the deceased ; and he sympathized with him to some extent, because he had been brought into the matter by his wile who appeared to be a very bad woman. There was no doubt that deceased died from the effects of a kick, and he thought the jury would have no doubt that the kick had been given by the prisoner with the clog which had been produced. It was not the first time that he had beard of R man who was a" bruiser " using his feet. In regard to Dr. Curtis, his Lordship said that no doctor in his senses would have performed an operation in such , a house as the deceased's surrounded as it was by dirt and disease germs. The doctor did his duty in advising the man to go to the Infirmary, which was clean and pure, and had the advantage of the newest discoveries , in regard to antiseptics, &c. No blame whatever was to be attached to,. Dr. Curtis, who was just as proficient in his profession as many other eminent men who had to , give evidence in these courts. And, therefore, he said, as he had said before, that there was not the slightest occasion for the attack which had been made upon him. The jury must say, under his (the judge's) direction, that the prisoner was not guilty of murder. It was for them to say, however,whether he was guilty of man-

slaughter. After a short consultation with his fello w jurymen the foreman turned to the Judge and said "We are in doubt whether these were two kicks or not, whether one kick was given by the prisoner and one by the woman." The Judge: It is quite immaterial whether there were two kicks or not. Tao wife says she saw the prisoner kick her husband. The prisoner was then found guilty of man- slaughter. The Judge, in passing sentence said no one who had heard the evidenco could doubt that the prisoner used

- great violence to the unfortunate man Swift. It was fortunate for him he had been able to take the lines he did in directing the jury, as he did no think the cir- CUMStaneeS of tke case justified him in finding him guilty of murder, but if a strong vigorous man like pri- soner, accustomed to active violence, used his fist or foot he must not be surprised to find himself in trouble. He should be justified in dealing with him less seriously than ac one time he thought would be necessary. Walsh would be seLtenced to five years penal servitude:

div.head: ONE FROM-THE WAR.
div.p: ONE FROM-THE WAR.

A Brave Veteran Interviewed, FROAf the wilds of Afghanistan to the depths of a coal- pit in West Monmouthshire is a tar cry, and there is a great differenc b3tween the glaro of an Indian sun and the gloom prevailing at the bottom of the Marine Fits at Ebbw Vale. Which of the two elements, the glare or the gloom, is the more unpleasant. we are not compe- tent to say, but there lives at No. 21, New Colliers Row, Ebbw Vale, a man who has had many years' experience of both, and he recently told an iateresing tale to a reporter who looked him up. It would mot need A SHERLOCK HOLMES

to tell that he had been a collier. The miner can gener- ally be distinguiseed by tiny blue marks on his features due to the blasting. These signs were apparent to the reporter who interviewed Mr. John Murgane—for that is the name of the individual referred to. At the same time his alert and straightforward manner proclaimed him an old soldier. Aeked for soma narrative of his varied experiences, "I am," he sad, " forty-five years of age, and have now been a collier for eleven years. Before that I was in the Army. I was in the 61st Regi- ment- 2ND BATTALION GLOUCESTERSHIRE. I spent seven and a ilea years in India, two years and nine, months in Malta and two years sod three mouths on the home service, making twelve and a half years altogether. The seven and a half years in India included two years in Afghanistan. I came home in January 1886, and was discharged en the 30th April 1888. "After coming home," he continued, " I was sent straight to Fulwood (Lancashire) Berracks,in the North- West of England, and joined the first battalion of the same regiment. The sudden change, coming from abroad and arriving in England in January, may have sowed the seeds of illness. When I left the Army I was all right, but every winter since I have suffered From liver cone- rlaint, and have been two or three weeks idle in conse- quence. Last winter I was again attacked in a worse way, and was practically idle for two months. I bed pains between the shoulders, and felt very laeguid and sleepy. I felt more tired in the morning than in the evening,after a day's labour. I was under medical treat- ment; the doctor called my complaint hepatic conges- tion (conges ion of the liver), and gave me come medi- cine. The medicine only seemed to purge and relieve me temporarily. My appetite remained as bad as ever —I had to force myself to eat." An Mr. Morgans, at the time of the interview, appeared to be in excellent-health, the reporter naturally asked what caused leis recovery. "I was recommended," be said, "by a woman living not far away, to take Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. I procured some of these pills, and commenced taking them. I took three or four boxes altogether. With the second box I felt relief, and when halfway through it I was back at work for the first time in eight weeks. I could then eat fairly well. I had gone down very thin." Mr. Morgans, who looked anything but thin, stated that he was not now as heavy as he once was—viz., be- tween fifteen and sixteen stone, but he looked quite robust and vigorous, and quite able to cope with his arduous daily toil. It is evident that the pills had not only improved his appetite, but also enabled him to de- rive nourishment from his food. "I do really believe that my recovery was due to Dr. Williams' pink pills," he said, and proceeded to volun- teer a remarkable statement. " I can safely say that in this neighbourhood Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people have done an enormous amount of good. The woman who recommended them to me—you could blow her down then, and now she is quite robust." " What did she suffer from ?" "She had asthma badly, and no doctor under the canopy of heaven could cure her, but she was made a great deal better than she had been by taking Dr. Wil- liams' pink pills." "Do you know of anybody else?' '1 Yes; there is a girl living in a house on the hill yonder who has reaped great benefit from Dr. Williams' pink pills. I was talking to her father yesterday. If you want any more testimony you had better go to him. They did his daughter a world of good." Especial importance attaches to the experiences of Mr. Morgans, both on account of his interesting and honourable career

IN THE QUEEN'S SERVICE, and also by reason of the useful lesson conveyed in his well-considered words. Either congestion or mere slug- gishness of the liver is responsible for many common ailments often not traced to this canae—such as bilious- ness, headaches, a sallow skin, pain in the back and shoulders, indigestion, and wasting from inability to obtain nourishment from the food. It will have been noted that ordinary medicine given to Mr. Morgans pro- duced a purging, and only did temporary good. A purgative has one use only.: It should be taken in order to clear the system ready for the really curative medicine. Dr. Williams' pink pills, by their beneficial effect on the blood, promote permanently a healthy action of the liver, and assist the absorption of nourish- ment. Thus they cure, not only chronic indigestion,but also such other blood-caused diseases as scrofula, rheu- matism, sciatica, and the deficiency of blood which in itself constitutes the prevalent disease ailmmia• Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, Holborn Viaduct, London, send the genuine pills post tree at two and ninepence a box ; which can also be obtained of chemists, and are also genuine when (and only when) enclosed in the registered pink wrapper bearing the full name.

div.head: PHILIPS' MILITARY MAP.
div.p: PHILIPS' MILITARY MAP.

By far the best war map we have yet seen is the large scale military map of the seat of war in, South Africa, which is published by Messrs. G. Philip aed Son, 30, Fleet-street, London, E.C. It is on a scale of 14 inches te the mile, and comprises two sheets, 35 inches by 24 inches. Sheet one represents the Orange Free State, W. and S. Frontiers, and Sneet 2, Derban to Pretoria. This Map has been prepared from the latest official sources in order to meet the need of a really detailed map on a large scale in convenient form. The two sheets cover the whole present and probable future scene of operations, extending from De Aar,Middleburg, and Sterkstroom to Mafeking on the west ; and from Durban to Johannesburg and P!etoria on the east. The general physical features of the country are graphically shown by means of contours printed in different colours, from the sea level up to 7,000 feet, whilst actual heights are given in figures wherever actually known. Kopjes, mountain passes, main mad cross roads are fully indicated. Rail- ways are printed in red with namea of all stations and sidings, telegraph lines are inserted from the most r-ceut official returns. Distancea of important towns from Durban, Cape Town, Port Elizabeth, and East London, together with their population are also given. Sites of recent engagements are distinguished. We may add that the map has been aperove,d by Colonel Mackinson, and copies of it were supplied to the City of London Volun- teers. It may be puschasrd at various prices, rangia,g from 2s. to 53. per sheet.
