div.head: BRABAZON SCHEME.
div.p: THE BRABAZON SCHEME.
Annual Sale of Work at Warrington. _

The object of the Brabazon iinploymerr; S3ciety which was tormed a few years ago is a most worthy otie—the intiroduction of some degree of cheerfulness and variety into the lives of the aged and infirm inmates of the Workhouses, which otherwise must be dull and msuo- tonous—by allowing them to spend some of their time in making various fancy and usefil articles. The scheme was introduced into the Warrington Workhouse in October, 1897, and the iesults have been excedingly gratifying,tne inmates taking uch pride in their work. The secretary of the local branch is Mrs. Edelston to whose painstaking work much ot the success achieved by the Society is due. On Tuesday afternoon, the second annual sale of the articles produced in this way was held in the Cou6cil Chamber at the Town Hall. There was a slight increase of the number of articles on sale on last year which did great credit to those who had been employed in making them. At the opening ceremony the chair was occupied by the Mayor and amongst others present were Mrs J Charlton Parr (who opened the sale),Mrs alelsten (hon. secretary), the Revs F E Powell, E R Tarbuck, and W H Drummond, Alder- man Fairclough, Councillor A J Jolley (chairman of the Board of (juardiats), Mr S Davies (member), and Mr George Thompson.

ANNUAL REPORT. Mrs. EDELSTEN read her annual report as follows:—"I do not think it necessary now to explain to anyone what is meant by the Brabazon bcheme ;it has been established at our Workhouse here since October, 1897. This is our second sale of work, and I hope it will be financially a greater success even than the first. I think myself, that the variety and good quality of the work before you reflects the very greatest credit on the poor workers—none of whom, you understand, are able- bodied, some of them bedridden, all infirm or disabled in some way. They take the greatest pleasure and pride in their word, and I feel sure that it has helped Co pass pleasantly many hours that would otherwise have been spent in monotony and weariness." Mrs. Eielsten here read the financial statement which showed expenditure amounting to £2O 43. 21, and re- ceipts £2 is. 10d. in excess. Continuing sue said You will see that we are quite dependent on the pro- ceeds of the sale to pay our warsand it is expected ot us that we repay as goon as possible the original grant from Lady Meath of £lO. Sc far we have only been able to reduce it by £l. We should be very pleased if we could pay it off altogether, and feel that all our income for the future could be spent for the benefit of the workers. Out of the proceeds of last year's sale we gave a tea to the Workhouse Infirmary—it was a very good tea, with spring onions and watercress—(laugh- ter)—followed by songs and a conjuring enter- tainment in the different wards. It was im- mensely apereciated ; we hope to do the same this year. I also put £3 aside to help deserving cases as they left the workhouse, and have spent about half of this. The

ladies who help in the work and come with most praise- worthy regularity every week are Mrs. Frost,Mrs Atkin, Miss Broadbent, Miss Coxon, Miss May, Miss E Birtles. Mrs. MoGragor has had to leave us, owing to ill health. We ti re very pleased with ourselves that wood carving has been recently introduced ; two men are doing it, under Miss May's guidance, and taking the keenest in- terest in it. Their first attempts are on sale to-day. The bent iron work is all the work of one man.who is suffer- ing from a very painful disease. I have no hesitation in saying that the introduction of this work has been a great benefit to the infirm inmates of the Workhouse—they are so much brighter and more cheer- ful than they were, and they enjoy very much the weekly vislta and talks with the ladies. They all take, especially the men, the liveliest interest in the war, and we have to keep them well supplied with newspapers. One man was very indignant at being put off with what he called " Graphics and pictures, and sigh-like," when what he wanted was the latest news." (Laughter.) They are as patriotic inside the walls of the Work- house as we are outside. (Hear, hear.) I should like to express my great indebtedness to the Mayor for so kindly giving me the use of the Town Hall, and for , being present on this occasion. I feel sure that this work has his cordial sympathy. I should. also like to
ill7a-n—k the ladies who are 'kindly undertaking the music

you will ehortly hear in the tea-roorn. Mr. Johnson for tea-tables lent, for the occasion, and for Mr. Connor for conveying the work free of charge to the Town Hall. We hope, as most of you know, to be in our splendid new Infirmary in the spring. and I trust that there the Brabazon sch,me will be allowed to flourish, and the ladies to continue their devoted work amongst the in- mates. (Applause.)
OPENING CEREMONY. The MAYOR said that before aolking Mrs. Parr to open ;he sale he would like to say how thoroughly he was in _
sympathy with thia work, and how from the beginning, when the discussion first arose as to the wisdom or other-

wise of introducing the scheme into their workhouse, his sympathy was entirely with, he was going to say, the veteran champion of the cause—(laughter)—Mre• Edelston. (Hear, hear.) How there could poseibly be two opinions as to the desirability of introducing an ele- ment of colour, however slight,in what must necessarily be the terribly grey life ei those who had to pass the remainder of their days under the conditions that obtained in our workhouses, fully admitting as he did all that had been done to make their lives as comfortable 1 and happy as circumstances would permit, he did not know. He approved of this scheme because it enabled the inmates to employ some of their faculties in a use- ful way, and he deprecated any attempt to prevent them so enjoying themselves. (Applause.) Mrs. PARR, in declaring the sale open, said the fart that so many were present showed that the public generally were interested in the scheme, and she was quite sure that they could not convey their thanks to Mrs. Edelsten and her follow-workers in a better way than by doing their utmost to make the sale of work a great succ9is. (Applause.) Sae had very great pleasure in declaring the sale open. Councillor A. J. JOLLEY propesed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Parr. He said that the name of Parr was always found to the front in every good work in connection with Warrington and district. (Hear, hear.) He took that opportunity of expressing his sympathy with the work of Mrs Edo:sten and her colleagues had carried out so successfully for some time past in the Workhouse. Without dwelling upon the debatable point raised by the Mayor, he could say that the logic of facts had shown the desirability of the work. Mr. Thompson, he might mention, had taken an active part in the inauguration of this scheme, and helped to secure its success. He always took a warm interest in the work calculated to be of social benefit. He (Councillor Joiley) expreesed the Guardians' deep gratitude to Mrs. Edelstein and to the ladies who had so devotedly given their time for the purpose of brightening the lives of the inmates of the Infirmary. (Applause.) The Rev. W. H. Deuerstmen, in seconding, theught they ought to thank Mrs. Parr and also Mrs. Edelsteo. Mrs. Edelsteo gave a great deal of trouble and time to this work. It was additional to the work she did as a Guardian, and that of itself required a considerable expenditure of time. He thought everyone who saw the work there that day would agree that it was calculated Ito do something to brighten the lives of the most unhappy of the inmates of the Workhouse. He thoucht it was not quite sufficiently realized that their workhouse hospital was to a large extent a borne for incurables among the very poor, and they ought te be looked upon as quite apart from the ordinary paupers who had brought themselves to the house by their own faults and evil doings. They were all exceed- ingly anxious to discriminate between the evil-minded pauper, who ought to be dealt with sternly, and those 1 who were simply the poor victims of their misfortune. (Hear, hear.) The report referred to the fact that in a few months the new infirmary would be opened, and he ventured to appeal to the ladies ot Warrington to show some kindly personal interest in the institution. Gifts of flowers, kc., were sent to the town infirmary, but the workhouse infirmary was treated with severe neglect. Gifts would be very acceptable. There was a limit to what the Guardians were allowed to spend in that direc • tion, but there was no limit in what they were allowed to receive from a generous public. (Langhter,and hear, hear.) The society's work daring the last year had been eminently successful in brightening the lives of the in- mates. .(Applause.) The motion was heartily carried. - Mrs. PARR briefly responded. The sale was then proceeded with. .....^............... Funeral of the late Mr. John Thompson.

The remains of the late Mr. John Thompson, sur- veyor of the Warrington Rural District Council, whose death was reported in our last issue, were interred in the family vault at the Parish Church, Knutsford, on Monday. The cortege left the resid- ence of the deceased at Orford in the following order :—First carriage containing Mr L rhompson (son),Mr Charles Bennie,Mr Fred Bennie(step sons); second carriage, Ur E C Cooper, Mr Henry Sander- son, (first workman employed by Mr Thompson, when he came to Warrington 33 years ago, and in hie employ up to the time of his decease), Mr. Newall, Mr. Smith (lirothers-in-law); third carriage. Mr B Newcombe,Mr W Wright(assistant surveyors), , Mr William Bate and Mr Thomas Silverton (fore- men); fourth carriage Messrs, I Maines, L Dumhell, E:Murphy, and William Birchall (workmen, who acted as bearers). The coffin, which was covered with a number of beautiful floral tributes from the deceased gentleman's family and friends, was of polished dark oak, with htavy brass moutings. There *as a large number of persons at the grave side, including the following members of the War- rington Rural District Council :—Messrs. Ball (chairman), William Honghton (ex-chairman), Mr Dignum, Mr firooks, Mr J C Sutton (clerk), Mr Kerfoot (inspector), and Mr Shearer. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
[By "Oval ist."l

Though they have net got the four points it was pos- sible to get against Widnes and Oldham, Warrington bave got two of them, and as those two were obtained at the expense c,,f Oldham there is not much cause to grumble. One supporter of the Warrington club twitted me on what he called my impertinence in suggesting that Warrington might beat Oldham. He had been quite overawed by the performances of the men trona Cottonopolis against Broughton, and Swinton, and for anyone to dare even to think of Warrington putting a spoke in their wheel was, in his opinion, pure cheek. I did not go so far as to say Warrington would win, but I stuck to my opinion that tbey could win if they tried, and the result has justified me in what I said. Oldham never do have an easy thing on at Wllderspool, and whenever they are going strongly for honours, then they know they must look out for squalls. So impottant was Warrington's win on Wednesday that perhaps I shall be excused it I deal with it first.

The performance was undoubtedly a magnificent one, for the Oldham men came prepared to do their best with the strongest team they could put in the field. War- rington were short of Smith, hie place had to te taken by Jones, who had not fully recovered from an attack ot,influenza. Immense interest was taken in the encounter, for Runcorn were taking a stiff job on at New Barns the same afternoon, and should the Cheshire men fall, and Oldham conquer the chances of the cup going out of this district were great. As it happened, Oldham lost and Runcorn won. The Warrington spectators rolled up in large numbers, not- withstanding that four o'clock is earlier than they generally finish work by an hour or two. Black faces and grimy hands told of the determination not to miss this, the match of the season. A good four thousand lined the arena when the combatants tripped gaily into the field five minutes after time.

The start was sensational, for after the ball had b3bbed about in midfield for a minute, S. Lees inter- cepted a pass meant for Jones and the Oldham men were soon speeding to the line Quick exchanges baffled the defeLders and a try was registered before 5 minutes had elapsed. This was enough to dishearten most teams but the Warrington lads never gave up. The visitors played with consummate skill and great energy but they were kept out and gradually tired down by the severe tackling of the home team. As Oldham slowed down, Warrington quickened the pace and were soon striving bard to wipe off the deficiency. A fine forward rush saw Taylor cross the line and come down with a crash when tackled by Fletcher. The try was not allowed and when the men sorted themselve3 out it was found that Fletcher had so strained his leg that he could take no further part in the game. Both teams had hard lines here, for Warrington appeared to have scored. Oldham maintained their lead until the inter- val, when Warrington were going great guns.

The "breather "appeared to benefit Oldham the most for they assumed the upper hand on resumption, and Sam Williams scored a beautiful try as the result of a superb run. It seemed all odds on the Ol ahem men now, for a deficit of six points is not easily wiped off. Warrington improved however, as time went on, and by three-quarter time they were showing great superiority all round. Some hard luck was experienced but at lazt Fish got through the Oldham defence in fine style. The score acted on Warrirgton as the smell of blood does on the tiger, and they threw themselves on the Oldham men with truly tiger-like ferocity. The tickling was deadly, and Oldham were steadily borne back. A scrimmage under the posts gave Warrington the chance required, and Eden scrambled over between the posts, Fish giving Warrington the lead by kicking a goal.

Warrington nut 8 points on in all)ut 15 minutes, and the p.,..rformance was cheered in a fashion we seldom hear at Wilderspool now. Oldham rallied gallantly when they saw the championship going, and until the close they taxed the home defence to the utmost. Lawton and. Isherwood had a most exciting race over the line after the ball, but the Warrington men won by the merest trifle. This perilous incident was due to a mull by Hallam, and never did he cause his comrades greater anxiety. A judicious mark or two by Bate soon brought the game to a close, and Oldham had to accept defeat by 8 points to 6..

There was not much difference between the teams. Oldisans's supericr finish and sped was equalled by Warrington's dash and determinAion. The loss of Fletcher. was of clurse, a severe blow to Oldham, but they had their share of luck in the first five minutes,and again when Taylor's try was disallowed. Zt IA not at all certain, eithor,whether Warrington would not have won if Fletcher had been able to play right through. The boys in "primrose and blue" were getting the best ef it before the international centre was laid out. There is no eainsaying the fact that Warrington's performance was a really fine one. There are few teams which could suffer a deficiency of 6 points against Oldham at threequarter time, and then pull the game out of the fire. Sheer doggedness did it.

On the Oldham side Thomas at full back played a grand game and saved his side time after time. Lawton and Williams were the pick of the other backs, the half tack being especially active. Most of the praise on the home side must go to the forwards, who retrieved their reputation thoroughly. Eden, Mere weather, and Taylor were ever to the fore, while Boardman did some streng scrimmaging. Bate and Burgess did splendidly behind the pack, the Fliston youth being tirelessly energetic. Isherwood and Fish were the pick of :the threequarters, who did web as a whole. The team still stand badly in want of a reliable full back.

There is not much to be said about the game at Widnes, where Warrington lost by 10 points to 7 points. The best team won, for the work of the Widnes fo:wards quite outclassed the Warrington men, who played care- lessly and without dash. Neither set of backs did any good work, but Warrington ought to have done better after leading at half time. They would have won had the forwards shaped like they did on Wednesday. The same thing can be said of several games which have been lost this season.

During the week, Runcorn have beaten Salford—after being behind at half time too—Warrington have beaten Oldham, and Stockport have beaten Leigh at Leigh. The League table therefore undergoes some alteration. Runcorn are now 6 points in front of Oldham, who have a match in hand. The Cheshire men ought to secure the championship now, and • they deserve it for their many fine performancer this season. To defeat Oldham, Swinton, Stoughton, and Salford on their own grounds is a feat few clubs ever accomplish, and yet Runcorn have done it.
The Lancashire League table up-to-date is as fol- ovrs : For.
Against.

To-day Warrington are at home to Rochdale Hornets,a team which took two points out of Warrington early in the sesson. Those two points ought to be got back and I fully expect that they will be. Beth teams have improved since they last met, but Warrington are undoubtedly the better combination, and have what advantage there is in playing at home. It does not seem to have been worth much to Warrington this season, for they have done better away than at home.

There are a couple of changes in the team, and it ought to be a little f•tronger than it wag against Oldham. Smith is down to take his place at centre again, Jones going back to the wing. SEARCHLIGHTS have been Imperial Dangers thrown upon some of the

dangers which beset the British Empire. We have to thank Sir H. CAMP- BELL-BANNERMAN for the light he has cast ahead and behind. It is for the nation to prevent the present situation from being used to foster wild and absurd ideas, to evolve vast organic changes, and to transform our Empire into one of military aggression and glitter. The rate of expansion of late has been very great. We have taken the other half of Burmah under our control. In China we have leased a new naval base and extended our acquisitions at Hong Kong. In India we have assumed responsibility for the military rule of Chitral and adjoining mountain valleys. In Egypt we have fastened ourselves on the country and ob- tained joint rule over the Soudan. In West Africa we have consolidated our position, and in South Africa there is little doubt that we shall make ex- tensive changes when the war is over. Every ex- pansion we make increases our military weakness and disorganises our military system. The political system must be affected in time. The Colonies have joyfully aided us in our present efforts, but they cannot be expected to remain in exactly the same political relations after the war is over. If the Empire is to be the stronger for ' this remarkable display of military enthusiasm, steps must be taken to organise the defence of the Empire on a new basis; and that will affect ' the political basis. If the Colonies are ready to take their share in the work of defence it must of necessity follow that their internal life will have to be accommodated to the new conditions. In a more serious war there will not be time to organise Colonial Contingents. They will have to be ready at once if they are to be of effective use, and this means training, preparation and expense. It also means some form of political co-operation and con- sultation. That form has yet to be devised. An Imperial Parliament in which the whole Empire is not represented is a misnomer. An Imperial Council may have to be constituted, and this must compel a reconsideration of our domestic institu- tions. Unity of defence may lead to unity of com- mercial regulations. It ought not to inspire in us a spirit of intolerance and aggression. As Sir H. CAMPBELL-BA.NNERMAN emphatically declared on Friday night, our Empire rests on peace, com- merce, and conciliation. We cannot pursue these aims and allow ourselves to become a swaggering military Empire. The danger to our finances has to be faced. If we are to reorganise ourselves on the Continental military idea we shall have to transform a good many other things. In any case, for some time to come, we shall be confronted with very heavy financial liabilities. Expenditure on the Army and the Navy is large and wasteful as it is, and the more we increase the sums annually voted the greater will be the danger of waste, bureaucracy, and domestic discontent. Policy determines expenditure, and ideas determine policy. It is important that we should hold fast to the primary ideas of Liberalism and progress. We cannot take over half the world, and rule it well and protect it properly, without effects upon us at home that will be serious, and may not all be satisfactory. False Empire may ruin us, exhaust our resources, destroy our commerce, undermine our respect for freedom, equity, and humanitarianism. Empires have risen, dominated the world, and declined. Their ambition has destroyed them. Warnings of this kind must Ito kept in mind. Upon the ideas and tendencies of the next years will depend the future of the British race and the British Empire.

POLITICANS who do not Mr. Balfour's Mistakes, read newspapers may be philosophers, but they are , not practical men. They are constantly losing touch with public feeling. They are apt to think that party loyalty will excuse anything. Mr. BALFOUR has had to be sharply reminded of his lack of attention on more than one occasion, and he does not seem to profit much by the lessons he receives. Upon whom he relies for advice at critical times we do not know,but he has a curious habit of doing the wrong thing, and in a helpless, inane way, as if he were really indifferent to con- sequences. His latest mistake adds to a consider- able list, and illustrates his cardinal weakness. The Committee he had off,red on the administration of the Patriotic Fund seemed to be likely to meet the general desire. But when he prlceeded to constitute it so that it should neither be Parlia- mentary nor Departmental, and to borrow only a few features from the former and none from the latter,he contrived to make as big a blunder as it is possible for any man to nsiak, under the eircum.

stances. He assigned representatives to the Patrio- tic Fund,but to no other perty in the dispute, his excuse being that he wanted the ingairy to be impartial. Mr. KEARLEY was omitted for precisely the same reason as one of the Commissioners was Put on—because he had taken a &finite position. Other names were added for same occult reason or Other. The impression left by the whole cast was One of evasion and avoidance, and there was general regret and consternation in consequence. NOW that complaint is so general, Mr. BALFOUR Seems hurt and surprised. The truth of the matter iS that he has insufficiently informed him self as to the nature and extent of the public dissatisfaction With the policy of the Patriotic Fund Commis- sioners. Probably, he has only given a slight, Casual, and perfunctory attention to the matter, instead of moving with care, scrupulous respect for public interests, and a desire to put an end to a public-scandal once for all. The result is a real blunder. Nobody is satisfied. With whom he Consulted on the subject we do not know, and on What Principle he selected the names, except in the ease of the two Commissioners, is not apparent. What he can expect from an inquiry so started we are equally at a loss to conceive. Tne public, he Should know by this time, has lost all con- s:ience in the ways of the Patriotic Fund Com- missioners. They have mismanaged some of the special funds entrusted to their charge. Instead Of aPending them they have hoarded them, and in this way the intentions of the subscribers have been defeated. No one who gives to a special eraergency fund intends money to be in hand when the objects for which it was started were well de- filled and have been exhaustively carried out. The Bufferers are the poor people for whom the money Was intended, and who have been receiving in- relief. The public is now giving more ra..,°lleY for war sufferers whilst surpluses of former gifts remain in hand. Such sums ought to be taacie instantly available for current needs. They "gilt to have been spent; but that is another raatter. The same p 011337, if allowed to continue, Will give funds in hand in years to come, when the need for relief will be dying out. Inquiry, under strong public pressure, may yet be directed _upon the right lines; but it will be in spite of M. -BALFOUR, and not in strict accordance with his "I ion. Stupidity of the kind indicated looks like ta,Ying a party game,but it is of the poorest kind. "'Dien public money subscribed for patriotic put-- Poses is wrongly used snubbing a critic is bad policy.

Warrington has of late been entirely given up 10 hero- i worship, which culminated this week n ° huge, impressive, and enthusiastic dereenstra- 'o23B in honour of the local Volunteers who are to the front. The Mayor, who rarely fails to -"/"“.3 the most of opportunities, organised a Patriotic public gathering in Parr Hall, for the 1341.1305 e of presenting the Volunteers with the held glasses and life insurance policies which have been i'llrehased for them by subscriptions. This event '30.1c place on Monday evening, being preceded by a.diener which was not unacceptable after the ser- i.°Lice ni church. We hope, sincerely, that the 'uoughts of the warriors, and guests too, did not :wander from the earnest remarks of the Rector to 4/le savoury viands which awaited appetite and PO digestion. Justice was, we think, done to both. Parr Hall presented a unique appearance, the floor being occupied by the tables and dinpeT, guests—amorie whom the " gentlemen in kharkt Showed prominently—while the spacious galleries and platform were packed by an enthusiastic mul- titude. Everybody who could get in got in, and hundreds came with money in their hands only to be turned away from the doors of a building which Was crowded to its utmost. The Volunteers were cheered to the echo on stepping before the Mayor to be presented with the tokens of Warrington's appreciation of their whole-hearted service to Queen and country. A fine body of men they looked, and we doubt not that they will form a Worthy addition to the ranks of the "Fighting Vortieth," our territorial regiment now with Qeneral Buller.

Warrington's leading strings have been of the lightest, and there will be some ?lief and thankfulness felt by the municipal thorities when the town, escapes from the bond rof the County Council. An inquiry was con- at the Town Hall last Thursday,when War- application was fully gone into. The ,4413ector, Colonel W. Langton Coke, appeared aa,v k! °llrably impressed with the case laid before b the petitioning counsel, Mr. Bradbury,and there Snot be permitted to judge from his attitude th,;' ~.618 not likely to be much difficulty thrown in "aY of the Corporation attaining its wish. 0 The application was not allowed to pass without _PPosition. There were no apparent grounds for Mr. TlZegh's objections; in fact it was a matter of eulty to decide whether he really had any. Mr. Gough did was to ask questions more less aimlessly and be answered with a curtness would have discouraged a less persistent in- ridual.Beyond expressing the opinion that he :Mt? little benefit to be derived from the change vrtposed, Mr. Gough did really nothing, and for- ttlOately, the success of the application does not ttePand on Mr. Gough seeing any benefit in it.

Century funds are very much in evidence just now. Three of the leading denominations of the ' Evangelical Free Churches Df this country have decided to mark the opening of the new century by collecting funds which in their total amount will approach, if not exceed, two millions sterling. The Wesleyan Methodists led the way with a scheme of one million guineas. The Congregationalists followed and appealed for half that sum and then with notable modesty the Baptists sot themselves the task of raising a quarter of a million guineas. Judging by the enthusiastic response which these several schemes have received there seems little doubt but that the whole of the amounts named will be raised. Daring last week the Baptists and the Wesleyan Methodists held public meet- ings in Warrington in support of the movement ; and the reports which were presented were in each case of a highly satisfactory character. The money is to be devoted to aggressive evangelical work This forward movement all along the line is dis- tinctly opportune at the present time if the stern Protestantism of the country is to be maintained against the insidious movements on foot to undermine it.

div.head: "SHALL RUNCORN HAVE A RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION ?" ---- Public Meeting.
div.p: "SHALL RUNCORN HAVE A RATE- PAYERS' ASSOCIATION ?" ---- Public Meeting.

A public meetirg was held at the Greenwav-road schoolroom, last Thursday night, with the object of solving the above question. The attendance was very small, but not discouraging, as the night was a terribly cold and bleak one, and many were prevented from at- tending. Mr. J. Meadowcroft, who was announced to preside wrote stating he was at the last moment unable to do so. He however cordially supported the move- ment.

Mr. Henry Dodd was voted tc the chair, and there were also present :—Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. J K Digees, G Hewitt, W Millington, John Capper, W Shaw,J Payn- ter, E Bowen, T Priestley, P Hopwood, W Bankee, H Grounds, G Duekett, J Hulse, T Booth, T Hunt, J P, ck, W Thornton, W Lawrence, W Powell, and H The Chairman, in referring to the object of the meet. int, said a statement had been eiven publicity in one of the local papers to the effect that the movement had been called into existence because •of the action of the Urban District Council in regard to the park scheme. He miebt as well tell them at once that such was not the case. So far as his knowledge went the fact that Run- corn was going to have a p Irk, and that a large sum of money was going to be spent upon it, had nothing to do , with the springing up of a ratepayers' association.Ae,ain, politics had nothing to do with it. (Hear, hear.) Tne statement that it was a Tory movement was absolutdy untrue. Those who were responsible for the inception of the movement, had not, at any meetings held, found fault with the policy of the Urean District Council. The policy of that body had not been attacked in any shape or form, nor had the policy of any individual member formed the subject of attack. In considering the question of the formation of a ratepayers' association, they thought the bast plan would be to make it as representative of the general body of ratepayers as possible. When the asso- ciation was properly launched it would be its business to consider the policy of the Urban District Council, and as to how far that policy met the views of the ratepayers. Personally he felt very strongly that they ought to have a ratepayers' association in Runcorn. They should re- tard such aa association not so much as a controlling power as a creative power. They wanted men in the Council Chamber whose policy they approved of. At present they only got a man's individual opinion, and that was a great drawback. If a member of the Council felt that he had the general body of ratepayers at his back it would give force and strength to his action on the Council. It would be the duty of the aseociatiora to approach candidates for election on the Council, and as- certain how far their policy was acceptable to the ass°. ciation. If the men they sent to the Council would not act in accordance with the ratepayers' wishes the asso- ciation would find men who would do so. He thought it was for them to do their very best in the matter, and to leave no stone unturned to bring the movement to a successful issue for the benefit of all concerned. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Bowyer proposed " That it is desirable a rate- payers' association should be formed for Runcorn." Dr. McKenzie seconded, and ob-,eryed that in the present Urban District Csuncil they had a House of L3rds, and if they established a ratepayers' association they would get a House of Conamons. They were the boys wbo could manage and rule the Council because they had to "fork" the money out. (Laughter,and hear, hear.) They had a right to s-e how their money was spent; he said that distinctly. They could only make the association a success by being thoroughly enited in the matter. Under the present state of affairs the House of Lords could "rule the roost," and there was a neces- sity for a ratepayers' association, not with a view of ob- structing the work of the Council but with a view of helping the Council and giving theca all the assistance they °out'. Mr. Priestley asked for information as b what bad losen done at the meetings which had been already held. He thought that whatever was dose, should be done on broad lines, and that there should be no " hole-and- corner" business.

The Chairman, in reply, said there were minutes of all the proceedings which had taken place hitherto, and anyone who wishes to see them could do so. The minute book was in the possession of Mr. Gerrard, of Brackley-street, who, unfortunately, had been confined to the house for a fortnight. There was us wish at all to make it a sort of "bole-and-corner" business. The movement was for the benefit of the wsrking mon of Runcorn, to which he and those present belonged. They desired that everything should be straight and above hoard, and that everyone should know what was being done. (Hear. hear.) The resolution was put to the meeting and unani- mously carried, _ _

Mr. J. K. Digges thought it ought to be thoroughly understood that the aasoeiation was not to be formed !with the object of fighting against the Cauncilibut rather to exercise a useful cheek on the spending powers of that body. He did not approve of spending public money on baths, parks, or cottage hospitals. He was in favour of them if the cost was met by voluntary contributions, and not from the rates. If the Council persisted in spending money on such things they mu3t give them to understand that they would be called to account by the ratepayers' association. (Hear, hear.) He thought a ratepayers association was a movement which should receive the support of tradesmen and working men. Mr. Digges moved "That the fallowing be appointed a pro- visional committee to draw up rules, arrange pre- liminaries,and report to a future raeoting:—Dr McKenzie and Messrs Walter Millington, T Hopwood, H Dodd,John Capper, W Shaw, E Bowden, J Paynter, T Priestley, and W Bankes." Mr: Hough seconded. _ _

The Chairman said, as he observed at the outset, there was no antagonism, nor had there been any, towards the Urban District Council. For his own part he had not one word to say against the District Council of Runcorn in any shape or form. The association, to be of any value at all, ought to make its infiumce felt at the annual election of district councillors. They would have to satisfy themselvee as to the policy of ;Aspirants for seats on the Council. and vote just as they approved or disapproved cf their policy. They would also have the right to call upon their representatives to give an account of their stewardship at the end of their term of office. If the movement sueceeded they would have no man saying he apoeared as a candidate at the request of a body of influential gentlemen, when perhaps that" body" referred enlv to one Or two men who had been asked to sign his nomination paper. (Hear, hear). _
The resolution was carried unanimously. It was resolved that Mr. John Capper should act as bon treasurer,and Mr. Walter Gerrard as hon, secretary pro tent.

Mr. Bowden made a vigorous speech, in the course of which he charged the Urban District Council with wast- ing the ratepayers' money for the last 20 years. Dr. McKenzie did not approve of a man being dictated to by the ratepayers, a great many of wham were illi- terate. If they were sending an intelligent man to re- present them on the Council they ought to let him work on his intelligence. The Chairman said he thought in /natters of policy the ratepayers had a right to be heard, and their wishes ouqht to be respected, The meeting at length terminated with a vote of thanks to Mr. Doll for his sorvices in the elair.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 23, 1900.

A RuNcoRN SCHOONER Mrssnra. Tho schooner Con;tance Mary (c i.pain J. Deakis, Runcorn), with a cargo of rick salt from the hip Canal, Runcorn to Charlestown is missing- The sbip left Sorno way a fortnight ago after a short 'Stay there through stress of weather, and :;,he has not since been heard of. It is thought probable that Captain Deakin has anchored in some bay on that rockbound coast, but some anxiety is felt for the safety of the vessel and crew.

RETIREMENT OF A VETERAN ST kTIONMLSTER. The London and North-Western Railway Com- pany is just losing one•of its oldest stationmasters in Mr. William Appleton. who has been fourteen years at the Great Moor-street terminus at Bolton. Mr Appleton, who is a native of Liverpool, was first stationmaster at Buxton and Runcorn and filled a similar position at Tyldesley. He has also been traffic inspector at Widnes, and a district police in- spector at Liverpool. His railway career embraces nearly half a century.

div.head: i RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: i RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT WIDNES.

Last Sun 'ay, John Meehan, 28, Church-street, Widnes, labourer at Bolton's copper vmrks, was ad- mitted to the Accident Hospital suff :ring from fracture of the base of the F,kull occasioned by fall- ing downstairs. He received careful attention from Dr. Hutchinson, and is slightly improved. BAPTIST CHAPEL BAZAAR, WIDNES.

The bazaar opened in the schoolroom attached to the above place of worship, on Thursday, was con- tinued on Friday. Mr J Gill presided, and the opening ceremony was performed by the Rev J Ped- lar. At the conclusion votes of thanks were accorded to the C:iairman and Mr. Pedlar on the motion of Mr. Routledge, seconded by Mrs. Crow. The total amount taken was about £43, which was, some ..E7 short of the sum required. This amiunt, however, in face of the weather which prevailed was very satisfactory.

div.head: DEATH OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.
div.p: DEATH OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

It is with regret wa announce the death of Mr. Peter Phillips, tailor and outfitter, of Church-street, which took place on Monday morning after a week's illness. Deceased was a victim of influenza, which is very prevalent in the town at the present time. He had been in business in Runcorn 16 years, and was generally respected by all who had transactions with him. He leaves a wife and two young sons to mourn his loss' and much sympathy is felt for them in thsir sad bereavement. The deceased was 41 years of age.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. LEADEETTER.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. LEADEETTER.

We regretfully announce the death of Sirs. Jessie Leadb3tter, aged 90 years, which took place at the residence of her sou-in law, Mr. Richard Moores,s3, Church-street, Runcorn, on Tuesday last. Deceased was a faithful member of St. Paul's Church. Run- corn, and a highly respected resident of the town, and though of such an advanced age had complete control of her faculties almost up to the end. The funeral takes place at one u',:iock to-day (Friday). FLAT SUNK OFF RIINCORN.—A MAN'S BODY SEEN IN THE RIVER.

On Monday as the flat " Bertie " belonging to Mr. R. Abel, Runcorn, was being towed up the river from Liverpool by the tug Helen, she was found to be in a sinking condition. The pumps were manned and every effort made to reach a place of safety, but to no avail and the flat sunk. Whilst the men were getting off the flat on to the tug they observed what appeared to be a man's body floating past, ani though efforts were made to recover it, the fast running tide carried it out of reach, and shortly afterwards it was lost sight of.
RUNCORN CADETS OF TEMPERANCE.-" GUIDE OF YOUTH" SECTION.

The usual meeting of this order was held on Saturday evening, in the Greenway-road School, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Whyte, who gave an encouraging address to a good attendance of members. Mr Daniel Bisbrown emphasized the importance of the menabirs keeping their pledge against the use of tobacco and intoxicating drinks, as it would be a safeguard and protection to theta along life's path. He referred to cases where men and women had been dragged down by intemper- ance. That temptation would have to be met, and he implored them to "Stand four square to every wind that blew."—The meeting then closed.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.

Coroner Dobson held an inquest at the Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of Mary Garner, wife of James Garner, labourer, Heath-road.—Evidence of identification was given by deceased's daughter Ellen to the effect that her mother was all right on Sunday up to dinner time. She ate an ordinary meal, and was afterwards given a cup of tea by witness. Subse- quently she complained of being unwell and having pains in the head. Dr. Robinson was sent for,but, did not arrive. Her mother expired very sqddenly. —Dr. F. McDougall, Runcorn, said he had made a post- mortem examination of the deceased, and from what he discovered attributed death to heart disease. —The jury returned a verdict accordingly.

div.head: NARROW ESCAFR AT RUNCORN STATION.
div.p: NARROW ESCAFR AT RUNCORN STATION.

On Friday morning, Charles Fish, employed as a cutter at Messrs. Unsworth Eros., tailors, Runcorn, was hurrying te get into a train at Runcorn Qtation, while the same was moving out, when he lost his footing, and fell between the edge of a carriage and the platform. Fortunately the carriage hap- pened to be the last on the train, and the man dropped on the permanent way. The train was stopped, and Fish was got into a compartment, and continued his journey to Liverpool in company with Mr. Howard, foremln Porter. He complained of having been crashed, but on arrival at Liverpool he was able, with assistance,to walk to his home. WESLEYAN MISSION SERVICES AT WIDNES.

Home missionary services were held in the Victoria Wesleyan Chapel, Viridnes,last Sunday,when sermons should have been preached by the Rev. Et W. Allen, of the London Garrison, but that gentle- man being!indisposed the Rev. Mr. Hocking took the services in his stead. There were fair congregations, At the evening service the choir gave a tasteful rendition of the anthem "Praise ye the Lord." In the afternoon Mr. flocking addressed the scholars of the Lacey-Ftreet School OR the work in foreign missions. On Monday evening the usual home missionary meeting was he:d, when Councillor Davies presided, and he was supported by the Revs. G.B. Saul and H. Barraclongh and others. Mr. Saul presented the report of the work done during the past year. Collections were taken on behalf of the Home Mission cause. Mr. W.Stanley presided at the organ,whilst Mr. E. 0. Evans conducted.

div.head: FUNERAL OF CAPTAIN BROWN, OF RUNCORN: • – – –
div.p: FUNERAL OF CAPTAIN BROWN, OF RUNCORN: • - - -

The remains' of the late Captain Peter Brown, whose sudden death on the Royal mail steamer Duke of York, while crossing the channel from Belfast to Fleetwood, was recorded in our last issue, wets interred at Runcorn Cemetery, on Saturday after- noon. The body was brought to Runcorn on Thurs- day evening, and taken te the deceased's late resi- dence, the house of his son (Mr Peter Brown, jun.), 24, Hope-street. The remains were followed to their last resting place by Messrs Thomas, Peter, Robert, and James Brown (sons) ; Masters Peter Brown, James Brown, and William Bratt (grand- sons) ' • Messrs Thomas, William, and Peter Gregory (brothers-in-law) ; Peter Burgess, William H Peacock, Thomas Riley, Joseph Riley, Reginald Peacock, Bert Peacock (nephews) ; J James, Charles Harper, James Armstrong, and Captain Hugh Hughes. The bearers were :—Captains A Millinger, John Ellis, T Dunhavand, and T Trimble. On arrival at the Cemetery the burial service was impressively read by the Rev W Scholes. A number of beautiful wreaths were contributed by the deceased's children Mrs Withington and family, Mrs Travitt, and Mr John Riley. The deceased was 70 years of age. He had followed a seafaring life since he was ten years of age, and was highly respected both by his col- leagues and employers. He had charge of the first vessel that berthed in West Rank Dock, Widnes, after its completion.

THE PEARL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. We have just to hand the annual report of the Pearl Assurance Company. Limited, for the year ending December 31st, 1899, and its perusal dis- closes to us a soundness and stability that will com- pare more than favourably with many Assuranta3 Companies. The increase in premium incoma has exceeded £lOO,OOO, the actual figure being :E109,371, whilst t'le increase in savings has grown by more than 36 per cent and last year reached the large sum of £158,170. The accumulated funds of the Company at the date of issuing the report are shown to be £1,000,000 sterling. Ia the ordinary branch alone the premium income amounted to £79,6B7,baing an increase of £15,806 over that of the previous year. New policies were issued amount- ing to £29,936 7s 6d, assuring the sum of £725598 The interim valuation as made by Mr. R. M.. Moore, A.1.A., up to December, 1899, showed a surplus of £147,099, of which the directors recommended £136,352 should be carried forward, and £10,747 distributed amongst the par- ticipating policy-holders. The total income for the year amounted to £764,262 151 ld being an in- crease of £111442 lls 2d over that of last year. The premium income on the policies in force amounted to £832,483 83 91. The Company paid 40,860 life claims and matured endowments amounting with bounces to £255,423 3s 74, which makes a total of £2.442,821 193 3d, paid in claims since the founda- tion of the Company. These figure.; speak for them- selves, and testify to the stability of the Company, and also to the steady advance and growth it is making. It is one the public can confidently trans- act business with,for in addition to general stability the company has a good name for paying its claims promptiv,a conaideration vrhieh should carry a long way with thoaa about ts assure. Mr. T. Gerrard, 50, Greenway-road, Runcorn, is the superintendent for this district, and any further information will be gladly supplied by him. div.head: FARNWORTH lIA.RRIER S , WIDMIS
div.p: FARNWORTH lIA.RRIER S , WIDMIS

On Saturday, at the Northern Cross Country Championship run at Rotherham, J Hosker, who is a member of the above club and holder of the championship, came in second to JD Marsh, Salford Harriers. Hosker took up the running, and main- tained a good lead for SOW, timP but in the end was beaten by Marsh by about 306 yards. The time of the winner was 66min. 3;ec.,.,, whilst Hosker's time was 66min. 42sec. FATAL BURNING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES,

A girl named Sarah Ann Trovetr,, four years of age, daughter of Joseph and Hannah Trevett, of 2, Earl-street,Widnes,died early on Wednesday morn- ing at the Accident Hospital from burns received on Tuesday. About 7.43 yesterday morning Mrs. Trevstt left the deceased and a younger child in the kitchen while she went to take her husband his breakfast. Shortly afterwards the deceased's grand- father, who was ill in bed, heard screams coming from the direction of the kitchen, and on running downstairs he found the deceased's nightdress on fire. He extinguished the flames,and the child was taken to the hospital where she died as stated.

div.head: MERSEY MISSI3N WEEKLY CONCERT.
div.p: MERSEY MISSI3N WEEKLY CONCERT.

The programme, which delighted the audience at Mersey Mission. on Tue,day evening last, Was made up ga under :—Pianoforte duet, "Caliph of Bagdad," Misses B and E Johnson; part song, "Now pray we for our country," Parish Church Choir; recitation "Somebody over there," Miss E Turner; instru- mental trio, concerto, Miss B Johnson, Messrs Savage and Craddock; song "One of she Queen's Naves," Miss E Johnson; madrigal, "Soldiers brave and gallant be," Parish Church Choir; humorous medley," The gallant Duke of York," The Choir Boys; cornet solo, "The Lost Chord," Mr J Clare; sentimental song, "The un-commercial Traveller," tr Shallcross ; solo and chorus, "Come if you dare," Parish Church Chair; duet, " Excelsior," Messrs Temple and Shingler ; recitation, " Praise of the bayonet," Miss E Turner; song, 'For Queen and Country," Mr John Pennington; Comic sketch, "The Phonograph," Masters Miles, Gibbs, Burton, Wilkin- son. and Hill; pianoforte solo, "Cascade of Roses," Miss B Johnson ; patriotic song, "The Soldiers of the Queen," the Choir Boys; humorous sketch, " Varieties," Master W Howard; nautical glee, "Rule Brittannia," Parish Church Choir. The efficient accompanist was Miss B Johnson. There were numerous encores, and the concert throughout reached a high standard. Votes of thanks were accorded the artistes on the proposition of Mr. W. Shaw. seconded by Mr. Rodd. The singing of the National Anthem brought one of the most enjoy- able concerts of the series to a close. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN ODDFELLOW.

The usual lodge meeting of "The RO3O of Sharon" Lodge (Grand United Order of Oddfellows) was held on Saturday night, at the Foresters' Hall, Devonshire-square. Bro John P Parr presided over a goad attendance. After the transaction of the routine business a long and animated discussion took place as to the relief of distressed members at a distance, and the retaining of widowe on the widows' list when contributions were in arrears. Bros. Davies, Douglas, Booth, and Rutter took part in the discussion. Bro George Rutter presented his report of the district meeting. Re stated that the society was miking great progress in numbers and funds and informed the ' members of the resolu- tions passed by the district for the better working of the society. After the initiation of several new members, Bro Hindley called upon Bro Davies, as the oldest member present, to hand over to Bro Douglas a jewel of the order, inscribed as follows :—" Presented to Bra J Douglas by The *RoRe of Sharon 'Lodge, in recognition of 27 years' faithful service as assistant secreta-y and treasurer". Bro Hindley said there was no need of words to describe Bro Douglas's work, or for a long story to be made of it. He had worked 27 years, and those who had seen his work appreciated his services. The jewel was only a small token of their apprecia- tion of the services rendered and the vast amount of work he had done in the lodge.—Bro Davies, in an interesting speech,full of amusing reminiscences, also referred to the valuable services Bro Douglas had rendered. He had worked with him as secretary during 27 or 28 years,and their connection had been pleasant and agreeable. On behalf of the lodge he expressed their appreciation of what had been done. and trusted their brother might live many years in health, happiness and prosperity, to wear the jewel new presented to him.—Bra Douglas thanked the members for their gift,which he deeply appreciate.i. He had taken a pleasure in the work he had done for the lodge. It had been done in a pleasant and agreeable way with those with whom he had to work, and he should he pleased to continue to serve the members in the future to the best of his ability.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.
Parochial Party. The Resignation of the Vicar.

On Friday evening a tea party, concert and dance, were held:in St. Mary's Sunday Schools, Great Sankey. About 150 sat down tø tea, after which Dr. M IrrlY (People's warden) alluded to the retirement of the Vicar. Many of those present he said, c >uld well remember his coming to the parish twenty-one years ago, and a'l had eojoyed some years at least of his friendthip, guid and ministry amongst them. He ay.is sure he Yole'ld feelings of all the parishioners when he said they were heartily sorry that the Vicar's health had cempellel him to be so little with them, and now to cause him to sever his conneotion with the Parish. At a meeting of the officers of the church it was decided to present an address to the Vicar, on behalf of the parishioners on his retirement, and he, Dr. Murray, honed that as many as could sign the address would do so. The address read as follows: "To the Rev. Elwin Sandy's Jack3on,M.A., Dear Vicar,--Your resig,natioa of your position as vicar of Great Sankey has occasioned much rorrow and genuine regret to all your parishioners and your many friends in this neighbourhood. Look- ing back upon your long ministry of nearly rtwenty-one years, we find on all sides evidences of your devotion awl careful attention to the wants of the parish. The restoration of the Parish Church, the ' erection of Sankey Sunday Schoels,sit St. Mary's Mission, ' Pen troth, of the commodious new vicarage, the *cquith- lition of rho Cemetery, and of the Infants' School in Pen- keth ; all these are to us lasting testimonies of your un- tiring energy and self-sacrifice. Your attention to your spiritual duties while health remained to you, your kindness to and thoughtful consideration for the Door' your devoted administration of comfort to the sick and dying ; all these special features in your character now recur tan 3 with a happy recollection cf the past, and a keen pang of impending lees. We wish nay: to record that in yela we all have had a friend in need and a friend indeed. That you in your retirement from your active serrice, will always be richly blessed by the presence and support of Him to whom you yeurself have so often and so eloquently directed our hearts' best thoughts, this will aver remain the prayer and sincere hope of your parishioners and friend; in the parish of Great Sankey." The address having been presented, The Rev. E. S. Jackson returned his thanks. Flo aaid he sincerely regretted that he was forced to relinqul3h his work there, and thouvhta of his " cure "there will aka ays he remembered with a pleasure for man 7 friends acquired, and with much regret for their loss by his resignation. His heartiest tanks were due to all who helped him in the pariah work in church, and in ShhOoli.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT.] Those people,—chiefi; boat pevle—who prefer payiag fines of 5s to furthering the education of their children, would do wall to pause and pze upon the mischief and damage which results troon their action; and, having done so, might compare with it the inestimable benefits which would be brought about by a little self-sacrifice en their part. On tne one hand, they have ignorance,with all that follows in its train; whilst, on the other, they find comfort in the fact that they have done their duty, and in knowing their children are the light and joy of the home, and have a prospect equal to that of I any other child.

The formation of Ra ate.payers' Association for Runcorn, is now almost an accomplished fact. A meeting was held last week and the question" Shall Runcorn have a Ratepayers' Association ?" was asked and answered in the affirmative. This is by no means the first time an Associltion of Rate- payers has got upon its feet at Runcorn, and the fact shoul -1 be given its due weight, by the body which is just launching out. I have to dissuade the Association from forming upon any lines but those of a tradesmans' a property owners' or influential townspeople's Association, in the hope that some- thing after the nature of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce would be attempted. My argument has been that only those people who have a great deal at stake will be likely to" carry weight" and accomplish real good. The workingman is all very well in his way; but, we know, from bitter experi- ence, what his ways are; and he generally leaves the work to other people, and simply exercises his prerogative as a grumbler.

The criminal classes of Runcorn may beware, for their old friend, Detective-Sergeant. Samuel Gregory is once more about to descend upon them. In his wisdom, the Chief Constable of the Cheshire Con- stablary, has made sundry changes, and the one that most affects Runcorn is the return of Mr. Gregory, whose place at Altrincham will be filled by Acting Sergeant White, of Runcorn. Sergeant Gregory when a constable at Runcorn, by his oblig- ing and kindly manner, made many triends and these heartily welcome his return.

There is a great deal of sickness prevalent in the district, but whether it is traceable to" bad drain- age "is difficult t 3 tell. Still we have such things as "bad drains "even in Runcorn, and olfactory evi- dence of the fact is not wanting, to anyone who strAls the streets of Runcorn. Possibly those re- sponsible for locating" bad smells" do not happen to pass nat way whilst they are on, or else ney would be promptly removed.

Of one fact, however, I have been assured, and that is that the prevalence of sickness is not at- tributable to the Runcorn Water Supply. The other day I had a conversation on the point with one of the most prominent of Runcorn's public officials, and he told me distinctly that the water though possibly not the very best obtainable was goad, wholesome, and fit for domestic use. Moreover, said he "I would never be a party to conceal any- thing from the Runcorn public, and if there was the least danger to fear from the water they should know at once." fhis is a candid statement, and whilst we have such a man to keep an eye upon the analyses of our water we can rest comfortably, feel- ing sure that warning of danger will be duly given, should the occasion arise.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Anyone seeing the game at Runcorn, on Saturday would not wonder at the result, but they would wonder how St. Helens ever got into the position they hold in the league table. They lack ability es footballers, and seem to depend entirely upon "brute-force." It does not always come off, how- ever, and on Saturday they learnt it to their sorrow.

"I am not going to say that the "red tails"' were all "angels," for they were not; but, I will aver,that "Saints "is a misnomer for the "Helenites." Run- corn taught them the object lesson—the great object lesson—which all football clubs have to learn which try the " brute force" argument, i.e., that two can play at that game.

What will be the result of the next encounter at Sr. Helens shoula not be hi doubt at all. Runcorn are by far the best team and should win by even a greater margin of paints ; for the weather promises to be more propitious for footballer, and conse- quently better opportumtios of scoring will ba afforded.

Runcorn's defeat of Salford plus the fact that Warrington brilliantly defeated Oldham has made "championship honours" for Runcorn, almost a certainty. However, we must remember " there's many a slip twixt cup and lip," and must therefore endeavour to win right to the finish.

div.p: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON.
ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN STATION.

On Saturday night abont half past nine a man named William McCorn2ac, a machine man em- ployed by Messrs. McCorquodale and Co ,and living at Newton was crossing the line at Earlestown station for the purpose of obtaining a ticket for Newton, when he fell on Lie line, and was unable to rise, lie was picked up by some of the officials and as it was seen that he was badly injured, he was removed on the ambulance stretcher to Dr. Mouncey's, where on examination it was found that he had fractured the knee cap. Dr. Mouncey at once ordered the man's removal to the Liverpool Infirmary, and he was taken there as soon as it was possible.

div.head: INQUEST AT EARLEST3WN.
div.p: INQUEST AT EARLEST3WN.

At the Town Hall Flarlestown, on Tuesday morn- ing, Mr Brighouse, coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of a woman named Stokes, 66 years of age, of Viaduct-street, ICarlestown, which took place on the 17th inst.— From the evidence given by Thomas Stokes, hus- band of deceased, an 4 Sirah Harrison, of 92 Regent- street, it appeared that deceased fell in Regent- street on the 9th int, owing to the slippery state of the roadway. Stokes went to the assistance of his wife, but she did not complain of any injury until five days afterwards.—On the 15h he called in medical aid, and it was then found that she had fractured two ribs. Despite every attention she gradually grew worse and died two days later.—A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The quarterly meeting of this Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown on Monday evening. Mr. D. Forrester presided and there was a fair attendance of members. The report and the statement of accounts showed that the cash receipts for the quarter were £B9lB 12s 01, being a decrease on last quarter, which was of 14 weeks, of £169 5s 8d but as compared with the corresponding period of last year showed an increase of £l7Bl 17s 81d. The net profits realised were £1335 us 4%d out of which it was proposed to pay a dividend of 3s in the to members which will require £1295 14s Od. adding £2O to the contingent fund and the balance £l9 17s 41-d to the dividend reserve fund. Daring the quarter 46 new members had been admitted, 13 had withdrawn, leaving 1525 on the register. 1084 of whom had brought in checks. To- wards the cloe of the quarter the Society began to supply coal in bags,and they were pleased to report that this new undertaking bore evidence of success already. The report was unanimously adopted. Mr. D Forrester was re-elected president. Mr T Houlden was reappointed audit,r and Mr T Cave as stock- taker. A grant of £2O was made to the local War fund, A donation of £5 53 Od was made to the Southport Convalescent Home. Unler rule ten authority was given the Committee to have the use of £2,500, to be appropriated by them in the fur- therance of the busineis of the Society.

Forthcoming Visit of Mr. 0. R. Cairns

Mr George Rotrart Cairns, of Ceicago, missioner for the Federation, will conduct an evange- listic mission in Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-straet, from Sunday next (March 4th) to \larch 9th, in con- nection with the church and the P.S.A.. Society. Mr Cairns has been a most successful evangelist, having visited Europe six times. He was born in Illinois, and spent the early years of his life there. He took a course in the State Normal University, expecting to fit himFelf for a teacher in the public schools. In the midst of this training he felt a strong desire to become an evangelist. Being gifted with a talent for song, he commenced his work as a Gospel singer in Texas, with Maj. W E Penn. They had immanEe gatherins in a tent seating five thousand people, and often this was too small to hold the crowds that came to hear the Gospel. In three years, under united labeurs, thousands professed conversion. Mr Cairns, by invitation, then visited Great Britain in the autumn or 1885, going first to Scotland, then on to England. In Nottingham especially he was greatly blessed. Here he mat the lady who afterwar,la became Mrs Cairns, who was then engaged in mission work in that city. After returning to the United States, Mr Cairns began evangelistic work alone, and has continued ever since with great success. Particulars as to times of meetings, Sze., are given in our advertising columns.

Warrington Field Club. At the ninth meeting of the winter session, held in the Museum Lecture-room, Mr. F. Emson read a paper on " Fishing Notes: the Pike." He com- menced with a suratnary of the allusions to this fish in the Latin and earlier English writers, and pro- duced evidence that some of the mediaeval ecclesi- astics, to whose testimony on gastronomical sub- jects a high value is deservedly attached, esteemed the pike above the salmln as a food fish. As against those authors who have deemed that the pike has been introduced from the Continent within histori- cal times, Mr. Emson defended the belief that it is indigenons to British waters. Touching briefly on the anatomy, rate of growth, and mode of reproduc- tion—about which latter the most preposterous beliefs have been accepted by men otherwise of sound mind—the lecturer passed to the practical parts of pike fishing. He exhibited specimens of the apparatus which the lover of this form of sport uses, and maintained that, despite their formidable appearance, the hooks inflicted little, if any, pain. He did not put an Esocian witness into the box to prove that it did not hurt ; but the evident sincerity of his own faith and the innate propensity of man- kind to accept unhesitatingly comfortable theories. combined to secure the general approval of his hearers. The di.asident minority—where could the Field Club be without ona or even several dissident minorities ?—concurred with the rest of the audi- ence in the opinion that Mr. Itimson had delivered a most charming lecture, evidencing a keenness of observation and a healthy love of open-air sport worthy of heal( Walton himself.

with summarily.—From the statement of Mr. Browne. who proseeLt3d on bebalf of the N.6.P.C.C., it appeared that the prisoner was a cabinet maker, and used to work at Marsh's at Bridge Foot, and was in receipt of about 263 per week, but now he would not work, and was continually drinking. Had it not 13t.en for a son and a daughter who worked and gave their mother 14s between them per week the family of six children would have I been starved. On Tuesday mornieg primoner went out and returned in the afternoon drunk, with another man. When his wife went home about five o'clock he sprangl at her, and doe was obligf,d to leave the house. She had to borrow a shilling and pawn so no clothes in order to buy some food Amu,: eleven o'clock the prisoner went home again, and then his wife and children were in bed. He commenced to make a noise, ran upstairs, and broke three panes of glass in the bedroom win, iow and made his wife and children run down stairs and into the street. At the time it was snowing. Prisoner had twice been convicted of the same offence, and had had three months' imprisonment in each case. Prisoner's wife gave evidence, and said that her husband had given her about 104 in six months.—lnspector Hackett, of the N.S.P.C.C., stated that he had had the case under his notice since June 1899. In November last year he visited the house in c)mpany with P.S. Evans. The children were badly clothed, there was little bedding, and there was no food in the house. He had warned the prisoner on several occasions.—The case of drunkenness and using threats was p oved by P.S. Evans.—Prisoner said his eyesight was not very good, and, therefore, he c3uld not work regularly.—Superin- tendent Monaghan said that this was the prisoner's 20th appearance for various kinds of offences and he was com- mitted to gaol for six months.

AN INGENIOUS FRAUD.—CASE FOR THE SESSIONS At the Warriiie"ton Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs T.Bizciteel (presiding) and J. W. Hayward Frank Thornton, a stranger, was charged on remand with stealing by meane of a trick from the shop of Wil- liam James Dunn, 36, Sankey-street at one o'clock on Friday the 9:h inst., ter° shirts, two sweaters, and a Silk muffler, valued in all at 18a 44.—The Clerk said that the prisoner w,s before the magistrates on.tbe previous Saturday and was remanded. Since then it had been ascertained that he had just come out of prison after serving 12 months for a Eimiear offence to that he was now charged with. Consequently he would have to go to the Liverp tot Sessions for trial. His last conviction was at Preston Sessions.—levidence was then called.— William James Dun. hoeier and gentieenen's outfitter, 36, Sankey-street, said that at one o'clock on Friday the 9th inst., the prisoner came into his shop and asked for two shirts, two sweaters and a silk muffler, saying that he had joined the Warrington Cycling Club. He supplied him with tire articles produced and told him the price. Prisoner then said he had not suffi- cient money with him and asked him to address the parcel to Mr. Jone 3, 43, Wilson P.ttten-strect, and he would pay on delivery. Leter on witness sent his son with the parcel and in conaiquenes of what be told him he went to 43, Wilson Pi ten-street and found that no one of the name if Jon s heed theze. The articles pro- duced were the sans^ as those he supplied to the Prisoser and their value was 181. 41.—Frederiek Dunn, 14 years of age, son of the last wirvese, said that on the 9:h Feb. his father told him to take a pereel to Mr. Jones, 43, Wilson Patten-street. When be got near tee house the prisoner met him and mired if he had brouglet a puce' from Mr. Dunn's. On his r-elying in the affir- mative, prisoner said he wanted some morn things and he would pay for lee goods when he ordered the others. Prisonc: teen went into a gateway instead of going in the house—Edward Pyet. terin,ger for Edgar Valentine Morten, 64, Winvoiele-street, said that between two and three o'cioek on the date in question, prisoner came into the shop and offarod te:o shirts and two sweaters in pledge. He asked 7s 61 for them. Witness asked him how he came iete possession of the goods and he said he had been wired for from Loudon. He said he was an electrician, and produced some wires. Witness ultimately lent him 5s 61 on the goods, which were sub- sequently handed to Detettve Meacock,—Detective Meaceek said that at nine o'clock on Saturday morning, the 10th inst., he apprehended the prisoner. He told him be was a detective, and that he (prisoner) was wanted for stealing goods by means of a trick He replied "1 know 1 have dente veronee" He took him to the Police Station aid fourd the mu-flier in his possession. He charged him and he replied" I am very sorry for what I have done"—Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial at the Liverpool Sessions. TRAVELLING WITHOUT PAYING THE FARE.

At the Warrington Police Curt on Monday, before Mr. Birchall aad ether rnegisteates, Michael Joseph Charnock, Sankey Old Hall, was summoned for travell- ing on the Ch.-shire Lines Railway from Warrington to Altcar and t. om Altcar to Warrington without pre- vicuely paying the fare with intent te avoid payment,on the 30th January. He was also summoned for a similar offence on the Ist February.—Mr. Forshaw appeared for the defendant and pleethel guilt:in Mr. Simpson repre- sented the Railway- Company. He said that the defendant formerly held a contract which expired on the 31st October 1899. Ile did not renew it nod instructions were given to the ticket collectors to keep a look out for him in consequence of something that had taken place previously. On thr 30th January he entered a train at Warrington and asked the ticket collector to tell the guard to stop it at Altcar. He did not take a ticket and did not give one up at Aitcar. He returned to Warring- ton the same eight without obtaining a ticket and on arrival at Warrington paid excess fare from Widnes. On the let February, he repeated the offence. When asked for a ticket at Altcar he gave up one which was inued on January 27h. On returning from Altcar he again paid the fare from Widnes. He was asked by the collector if be had not corns from beyond Widaes and he said he had not. Altogether he had defrauded he Cernpany to the extent of about 6a.—Mr. Forsiia er, for the defence, said be was instructed that the derendant had no intention to defraud. His client had le-en in the habit of taking out a contract tieket hut had neeleeted to do no this time. Be was in negetlations to :4e:du one. On the dates in question he did pay the fare from Widnes but he thought Ir had paid it from Altear. He neglected to look at the receipts or count the cheege that was given to him. He regretted having cemmiteed the °Memo, it was the first time he had ever done so,and he assured the Bench that it would be the last time.— The ticket collector was called and said that he asked the defendant if he came from beyond Widnes and tie seici " No."—The Chairman said that disposed of tho stetemeet that he thought he paid the fare from Altcar.—A free of 53 and costs in each case was irnpeeed.—William White Murray, 86, Stamford-street, Old Trafford, Manchester, was summoned for travelling hem Manche3ter to Liverpool on the 18th Janua.ry, without paying the fare.—Mr. Fowler appeared or the Oel'endant who did not attend the Court.—Mr. Sirnpeon said the defendant previously held a contract which expired on the 31st December. When application was sent for a renewal, the old con- tract had to be sent in, but the defendant had not sent his although he had beee werttea to three times. In- structions were given to the ticket-collectors at Warring- ton to watch for t'ne defendant and on the 18th January he was seen in a first-class Compartment in the 4-30 train from Manchester te Liverpool. He was asked for his old ticket and he made an excuse saying he had not eel it with him. He was then asked for his fare (53 61) and he said be was goieg dews to Liverpool to make arrangements for a new contrect and " it would be in- cluded then." The colLetor demanded the 51 61 taut he refused to pay it. He was then asked for his address and be said he was living at the seme address at Irlane. He went on to Livrepael but did not go to the Manager's office and up to tne present time bad not paid the 53 61. it was also found that he had not been living at Irlam for three months. They had great difficuly in dis- covering his whereahe .t 3 but he was eltimaeely found to a,e living at Oel Traff arc), Manchester.—Mr. Fowler said that the defendant had been travelling for his firm lately and had net had the cpportenitv of getting a con- tract. A fine ot 20s and costs (22 7s Ocl in all) was imposed.

- Smethurst and Mr. J. Heptierd.. VIOLENT ASSAULT.—A.rthur Taylor, 13. Irlrria-street, pleaded guilty to assaulting Walter Stanley Lazenby. 11; Irlam-street, on the 9th February.—Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins appeared for the camplainant. He said it seemed that a short time ago Lazenby accidentally knocked down a gate belong- ing to the defendant. As a result of a conversation between the complainant and the defendant's wife it was arraaged that a certain slam should be paid for the damage done. Matters went oa for some time and Lazenby did not pay the contribution which had been agreed upoa. Lizenby went into the defendant's shop, and it appeared that the defend- ant lost his temper and struck him a most v.elent blow in toe mouth with his fist.—A fine of 20s and casts was imposed.

Hayward and H. T. Fairclough. POLICEMAN AsAULTED.—OWeI Barry was chargei with being drunk add disorderly at Mar et-zato at 12,33 tho pre- % ious day, and with asiailltiug PC. Berinett.—fhe officer gave evidence to the eft,ct that he was on duty at Market- gate when the prisoner came up, and without the slightest provocation, struck him a violent tlow in he mouth with his fist, causing his teeth to bleed aud hi i lip to swell With the assistance of P.C. Taylor, be toak the man to the Police- station.--Prisoner, ho gave no reason for committing the assault, was sent to gaol for two months with hard labaur.
lioNDIr —Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Conno,illor

Smethurst and Hr. S. Wright. WILFUL DAMAGE.—Martin. Dooley, last from Liverpool, was eliarg.,d with wilfully breakillig a pane of glass in the window of the house Igo. 42, Hale-street, and also with dam- aging the blind and window to the extent of 4s. He was further charged with using threata towards Thomas Connor, at the same time and place and with wilfutly breaking a door panel and a lock staple at 3 33 on Saturday night. -Connor, who is a carter, said that at 7-45 on Saturd ly night he and his wife went out and on their return they found the door panel had been kicked in and the lock staple broken. They were told that the prisoner had committed the damage and he reported the matter to the police, Later on the prisoner came to the house and threw a large stone through the win- dow. He also threw a stlne which nearly hit witness on the head, and threatened to take his life. He was subsequently taken to the Police Station.—P.C. Corbett slid that at one o'clock on Sunday morning he was on duty in Orford lane when he heard screams from the direction of Hale-street, He proceaded there and on approach- ing the house of Conner he Baty Hrs. Connor stand- ing in front of the prisoner who was making use of filthy language and threats towards the last witness. Witness subsequently found the large stone produced in the kitchen of the house; prisoner having thrown it through the window. A panel of the door wis kicked in and the lock was damaged. Prisoner was under the influence of drink but knew what he was doing.—Prisouer was ordered to find two sureties of £lO each to keep the peace for six menths(or in default a month's imprisonment) for making use of the threats and for com- mitting the damage was sent to gaol for a month. UNSTAMPIED bCALES.—Thomas Booth, Pinners Brow was- fined 108 and costs for having unstatnped scales La his posses- sion for trade purpoaes.—lnspector Pl4.ze stated the facts of the case, and Inspector Wallington gave evidence.

SINGUL R CONDUCT.—George Purchase,last from Liverpool was charged with stealing from the door of the shop of Messrs Freeman, Hardy and Willis,Sankey-street at 9-50 on Saturday morning, two boots value is lid their property.—He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Monaghan said that the boots in qu stion were odd ones. At the time named the prisoner went to the shop door took the boots, and walked straight to the policeman on duty at Market Gate and told him he had stole,. them and wanted to be locked up He was taken to the Police Station.—The prisoner : I hope the magistrates give me a long sentence.—The Clerk: Why do you want a long sentence? Prisoner : lam better in prison than out.— The Chairman Have you been in prison before ?—Prisoner: No sin—Superintendent Monaghan He says that it is six months since he had any work and I can quite believe it.— The Chairman: Wh7 don't you work ?—Prisoner : I can't get work.—The Chairman said that work was very plentiful —The Bench decided that as prisoner would not work out: side he would have to work in gaol and committed him for three months hard labour.—Prisoner : Thank you.
