div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Widnes Beat Warrington.

Widnes and Warrington played their return fixture at Lowerhouse-lane, Widnes, on Saturday, before about 4,000 spectators. In toe first encounter Warrington won by 6 paints to 5, and the Widnesians were determined to wipe out the defeat. Toe weather was highly satis- factory, and considering the amount of snow which had ' fallen during the week, the grauad was in excellent order, then& heavy for running. Warrington were short of Jouee through illness, and his place was taken by Hoekenhall. Widnes were at full strength. The teams which turned out in charge of Mr. B. Ashton (+Nemeth) were composed as follows Widnes: Baty, full back; Brennan, Bown, Rispan, and Hughes, three quarters ; Douglas and Murphy, half- backs; A.spey, D onnelly, Kelly. Pougher, Leyshon, Hamp- son, Riley and Travis, forwards. Warrington : Elallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Smith, and Hockenhall, three-qaarters ; Bate and Bur- gess, half backs; Taylor, B ierdcnan, Mrtisun, Eden, Mereweether, Ssholtze, Fairhurst and Swift, forwards. Aspey started for Widnes, and after exchange kicking between Burgess and Rispan, the game settled in the Warrington half. Murphy got away from toe first scrim- mage and passed to Rispan, who in turn fed Hughes, the latter being promptly grassed by Hockenhall. Bown tried a drip at goal early, F.sh touching down. A couple of goad marks by Burgess kept the homesters at hay for a time bit they forced their way to the Warringtonline. A scrimmage was carried under the posts, and Douelas passed back to Hispan,wlao fallen at the easiest of drops. Bown then secured and a roar of applause went up as he dodged man after man of the Warrington forwards. Fish was too quick for him however. Then a mull by Hoekenhall lmost let Widnes in, Rispan knocking on badly. Burgess was instrumental in forcing Widnes back for by a short punt and run he pat Mtreweather on silo and Baty was bowled over in his own half. War- rington now began to have the best of matters, and Hockenhail twice tackling the home full back in grand style, Widnes bad to defend. Hallam had a kick charged down but Isherwood saved, Bawl' making an ineffectual attempt to thread his way through the Warrington team A moment later,Widnes were penalised and Fish landed a neat goal, to the joy of the Warrington partizans, who were in strong force. Just before the inters's.: B irgess came away from the pack with a grand dribble right to the line,and when a try seemed cer aiu the ball cannoned off the post into touch. At half time Warrington led by a goal to nil. Taylor r;-start d, and Widaes soon shoed that they meant tau ;Mess, Baty trying a penalty shot in the first five minutes. el m:s-kiet by Hallem ended in play settling near h Warriegton line, which was subjected to a i l. Chs hail was rushed ever, hut &viten- hall le-lecke-4. it against the fence just in tams. Widnes kept up th - pressure, and at last Bess missed a fly- kick and Murphy scored at the coiner. No goal follessed, but Widnes now lead by one point. The ‘Varringten forwaras fedeff in their play, sal the game prere-eded or e long time iu the visitors half. Rispan was givea a second nice chance, and this time he dropped a good pal. At last Warrington got into the home half, only to be sent deck with a rush, Bown dropping on the ball in the melee under the posts. Baty kicked a goal. The next two minutes were sensa- tional, for from toe kick-off Morrison got away, threw to Eden, and the latter romped under the VVidues cross- bar. Fish kicked a goal, and a try only separated the teams. Time was up, however, and Widnes won by two goats, 2 tries (10 points) to Warrington 2 goals, 1 try (7 points).

div.head: Warrington v. Oldham. Great Game.--Defeat of Oldham.
div.p: Warrington v. Oldham. Great Game.--Defeat of Oldham.

This return match, which sneuld have been played on February 10th but was pestponed owing to the frost, came off at Wilderspo 31 on Wednes lay afternoon. The weather was very suitable, and the ground had in a great meesure recovered from the snow and rain of the previous week. Warriugteri made ono change in the team which did duty at Widne3, Joaes appearing for Smith, who was injured. Toe visitors left inning to chance but broneht a full team, Though the match was a mid-weak one, the spectators rolled up rapidly, and there would be four thousand present: when the teams faced each other in charge of Mr. S. Williams (Salford.) Tree teams were as follows Warrington: flallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Joaes, and Hockenhall. threequerters; Bate and Burgess, half-banks; Taylor, Morrisou, Boardman, Eden, Mere- weather, Scholtze, Fairhuret and Swift, forwards. Oldham : Theeaas, full back; Davies, Fletcher, S Lees, and Williams, tare -quarters; A Lees and Lawton, half-backs ; Teller, Prater, Broome, Bonsor, Wilkinson, Sellars, Moffatt, and Porter, forwards. Jones started the game for Warrington' S. Lees re- turning to fial!am, wile punted finely andfollewed Lawton got possession, but Burgess dropped him. A minute liter a shocking pass to Jones saw S. Lees inter- cept, Fletcher, Davies and A. Lees carrying on the move- ment to the line, where the last-named scored. There was no goal. Lewteee again got away only to be bowled over by Hockenhall. Fletcher broke away, but was held. Burgess thee dribbled away through the Oldham backs, Eden tackling Themes. A penalty against Oldham was taken ineffectually by Fish. Oldhaea were very smart but shady work at the scrimmage lost them greiend. Davits dodged Hockenhell and sprinted down touch but Taylorestopped his progress. Then Williams got away from Lees' pass oaly to be upset by Fish. Istuirwood reeponded with a run and punt, but Thomas was sale. Lawton Fletcher, and Davies, ran down cleverly, but the wing man was stopped on the line. Prater took a penalty but failed miserably. A piece of deliberate covering of, Thomas by Davies was noted by the crowd but net by the referee. Warrington's defence was very good, but they made little headway. A grand pets of play by Morrisoa and Bate at last took play into the Oldham half, where Davies got a grounder. Frater relieved well, but Warrington were soon back again and playing with gem determination. Taylor got over, but was brought back for a knock-on. Fletcher was hurt in the rush and carried off. Davies went centre, and Sellars wing. Watrington scrimmaged under the goal, Sellars knock- ing on after geed 'Jasmine. Isherwood kicked to the ce:ner, Williams sending dead in the nick of time. Hell- time, Oldham, 1 try ; Warrington, nil. Moffatt restarted and Warrington dribbled back to the Oldham half, but bad passing lost them ground. Oldham combined well and for a time pressed Warrington back, Williams took the ball from a kick and outpacing the home backs scored in good pesitien. Sam Lees made a poor attempt at goal. Burgess punted down to Thomas who mulled near the line. A grand bout of passing by Lawton, S Lees, Davies and Williams nearly resulted in another try, Fish tackling well. The st endard of play on both sides fell off,Warrington having slightly the best of it. Fish nearly got in from Isherwood's pass, but the Oldham men tackled well. Warrington press 4on the line, Bate getting over after the whistle had gone. Thee ' smart passing by Bate Isherwood, and Fish, reaulted in the latter scoring grandly at the corner. He just failed at goal. Excitement now ran high. Grand passing by ' Warrington ended in Isherwood stumbling when near the line. Then Taylor charged down and dribbled to the line. From the pack Eden scrambled over. Fish kicking a goal. Tremendous cheering, followed the accomplishment of the feat. Isherwood got his men going again with a fine punt and follow-up. A mull by Hallam saw the ball rushed over, Isherwood falling under Lawton, on the ball. A serviceable mark by Bate removed play to centre. Davies and Williams came away with :a grand burst, but numbers prevailed. Lawton made great efforts to put a better complexion on the game. but the tackling was deadly. Oldham preeeed hotly, and Warrington had all their work cut out to keep their line intact. Oldham exerted every nerve when they saw their hopes of the championship dis- appearing, and were still attacking when the whistle sounded the filial, to the joy of the home crowd. Final score :—Warrington 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points) ; Oldham, 2 tries (6 points).

div.head: Runcorn v. St. Helens. A Rough Game.
div.p: Runcorn v. St. Helens. A Rough Game.

The visits of the " Saints," to Runcorn, attracted an attendance of about 5.000 to Irwell-lane, on Saturday, and speculation was considerable as to tLe ultimate issue. The" Saints" were short of three of their regular men, including the rethubtable Traynor. Bat the " Linnets" had full strength out, as they intend to run as little risk as possible, now their chances of " cham- pionship honours "look so rosy. The referee was Mr. Turner of Warrington, and be lined up the teams As under about seven minutes after advertised time. Runcorn: Houghton, back; C Butterworth, J Butter- worth, T Warder, and T Wilkinson, three-quarters; J Faulkner, and J Jolley, halves ; S Waiktr, El Farmer, F Tomlinson, A Taylor, Gayter, Lightfoot, 0 Hughes and T Darlington, forwards. St. Helens: R Foulkes, back; Hunter, Barnes, Cross and Doherty, three-quarters; Boyle and Appleton,halves; Winstanley, Prescott, Th.mpson, Briers, Moores, Dale, Rennie and Green, forwards. Barnes set the oval spinning, and the Saints were suc- cessful during the opening exchanges. The tide son turned, however, and Runcorn looked dat.gerous, whe Foulkes effected a clever save. Be got hurt in the rush that followed, but resumed. The Runcorn pack heeling

out well gave Faulkner the next opportunity, and though he imp7oved it considerably, his opponents were too keen to allow of his scorinz. Barnes replied, and Houghton was visited. In &Wine' the greasy ball he fumbled, and was soon collared: 'Smart wont followed en both aides. At this stage roughness developed con- siderably much te the detriineut of good football. &vocal players sustained sight iojuries, and cessation of play was frequent. Farmer, put a different aspict on affairs, by a eicely executed piece of buifiag,follo wed by a good run. Warder stopped his progresi,aad immediately afterwards the ball p tssA right along the Runcorn line, and resulted in C. Butterworth seorieg at the corner. Jolley tried to improve, from a difficult position, bit failed. Diversion next came from Farmer, who tried to I break away from several of the Saint-a. Following up the advantage keenly Foulkes was visited, and responded superbly. Jolley marked, and was isavily tackled and thrown by Wiestanley, ...with the result that th 3 latter was ordered off. Subsequently Foulkes fumbled and was held. From;the scrummage. J Butterworth was nicely fed by Faulkner and Jolley and scored a try. Tee kick again failed. At half time Runcorn lee by 8 points (two tries) to nil. From the restart, the visiting forwards suede a deter- mided attack upon Houghton, and showed more vigour than at any stage of the name previously. Jolley and Butterworth well supported their captain, and soon a raid was made on Foulkes. C. Butterworth got the first chance, but failed to take his brother's pass. oulkes, Green,and Hunter were next conspicious for St. Helens. Gradually, however, the" Linnets" were assuming un- controlable mastery of the situation, and soon had the Saints penned in their own territory. Briers tried, time after time, to raise the seige, but a too keen attendance of " myrtle-green" nullified his efforts. An exciting time followed, brought about by excellent play on the Run- corn backs' part, and following up a rush, 0 Hughes fall on the ball and scored thethird try for Runcorn. The game, was, thereafter, uniateresting save for a capital run on tne part oi Briers, wisich marked him as an ex cellent forward. Final result : Runcorn 3 tries k 9 points) St. Helens, nil.

div.head: Rev. J. Yonge and the Parting
div.p: The Rev. J. Yonge and the Parting
Volunteers.

Preaching in Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sun- day evening from the test "God is our Refuge and Strength," the Rev. J. Yonge asked was it not a sign of greatly rectified feeling that ‘ee were sending out our troops now in many cases, with memories of special services in the churches and cathedrals of the land ? It was not so at first. We then sent the troops out in all the pride and arrogance of our imagined power. We thought tint the army had only t 3 stelae itself in its mighty array of force, for the enemy to flee before it. Events had shown the felsenege of their hopes, the coin- plots erroneeuseess of their calculation?. We had had to learn the meaning of defeat. But there could be no question whatever that the nation had taken the lesson to heart and had very largely learnt it. P e3ple were coming to see that selenen religious seevicee of prayer and trust were the most befitting " Need-offs " for the men we were sending to the front. They in WarrinWon must have noted with satisfaction that a parting serviee for the volunteers was to be held at the Perish Church. The Rector invited the attendance of ail who wiabei to invoke God's blessing upon their eoldiere, That was a prayer, at any rate, in which all could elite ; very specially so for their own neight)ours, fellow townsmen, friends, perhaps telatione, who this week would go forth in the ceuerry's cause. Might he repeat that they at Wecliffe had direct personal interest in at least one of the Volunteers who were going. The church membership of Wycliffe would have its representative at the frent. Their prayers for the protection and upholding and comforting of their men would be all the more persistent when they remem- bered their young brother and they trusted that he might page through the fiery ordeal and return un- harmed. It was a good thing, further, to knoie that their men had been provided with suitable bibles. A bible in the soldier's breast pocket might beeeme a pro Eection. Any way a bible ready to the soldier's han would prove a priceless boon in hours of cuff Aring or o sickness, or in moments when suffering found its endine n death. God grant that the soldier's bible might bg he best prized blessing in his kit.

div.head: SUICIDE AT GRAPPENHALL
div.p: SUICIDE AT GRAPPENHALL
Inquest.

An inquest touching the death of Alice Brierley. aged 31, who was found drowned in a pit in Ball House-iane Tannery, on Friday afternoon, was c)aducteci at the " Parr Arms "Inn, Grappenhall, on Monday afternoon, by Mr H C Yates, coroner.—Mr. Jenkins was foreman, of the jury. The first witness was Thomas Briefly, of Lymm, who said that he was the brother of the deceased. On Thursday evening last the deceased and her father went to see him at Lymm abeue eight o'clock, and stayed until about 9.15. During that time he noticed that the deceased was rather peculiar ire her manner,and she complained of trouble. One matter that she referred to was that her sweetheart had not been to see her for over a fortnight. She said oho had had some words with him and told him not to see her again. Witness tried to " talk her round," and he went home with her and her father to Grappenhell, and when he left tint night she seemed cheerful and shook hands with him. About ten o'clock the following morning he heard that she was missing. He had never seen her so law spirited before. She had never expressed any in- tention of taking her life.—ln reply to the foreman of the jury witness said that her father took her to see him in order to effect a reconciliation, Thomas Ingham, a tanner, of Grappenhall, said that on Friday morning, about four o'clock,deceased knocked him up and asked him to go to her father who, she said, was ill. She was dressed in her nightdress with a fur round her neck. She was so anxious about him going at once that he went in his nightdress, covered with a shawl. He found her father sleeping and he left him, and went downstairs, and ho told the deceased that he should be left alone. She apologised for calling him up so early and he went home. She seemed rather excited about her father. He had known her all his life, but had never noticed anything peculiar about her nnaneer. Albert Wealley, of Appleton, said he had been en- gaged to the deceased for about fifteen months, and had known her about six years. On Sunday evening, February 4th, they both went to church and then she seemed all right. They were to meet areain on the Wed- nesday or Thursday, but that engagement was not kept because he received a letter requesting him not to see her again. She also seat some of the presents back that he had given her. Ho did not know what she meant, and he did not write to her or see her about it. During the time he bad known bet. he had never noticed any- thing strange in her manner. Here the Coroner read a letter that the deceavd left in her father's house for the last witness, containing the words" Even the sermon on Sunday I thought would touch you. My mind has changed. When I once get a thing in my mind it is hard to change. Ith tnk you for your kindness to me, and I hope never to forget it. God-bye. A. 8." P.C. Thomae said he received the information that the deceased wai miesing about ten o'clock on Fridey morn- ing. He followed her footiteps from the house to the wall of the B ellhoese-lane tan-yar 3. He emptied the pit nearest to the wall and found the body of the deceased. The eeall was a high one and probably she had climbed over it. She was a person who weuld not have anything to do with anyone.
The deceased's father havinz Oven evidencq. the Coroner summed up, and a verdict of " Suicide whilr, ternourarily of unsound mind " was returned.

An inqu3st was conducted by Mr F A Joae,3 deputy coroner, at the Midland Hotel, on Tuesday evening relative to the death of Richard Barrow, wire bundler, 63, Pierpoint-street. Deceased, who was 45 years of age, lodged with his nephew, a Mr Marsh. On Sunday night deceased and Marsh had several pints of beer in the house. Barrow went to bed about midnight, occupying a bed with a lodger named M`Donalcl. About 1.30 on Monday morning deceased got out of bed, and subsequently M`Donald was awakened by the sound of loud groaning. Ile obtained a light and found the deceased in an un- conscious condition at the bettom of the stairs. Dr. O'Donnell was immediately summoned and ordered the man's removal to the Infirmary. where It was found that he was suffering from a fracture of tLe skull. He died without regaining consciouiuess. A verdict of "Accidental death " was re- turned.

As Mr. Frank Turner, superintendent of the Fire Brigade, was passing along Gelborne-street at ten minutes past ten on Monday morning he saw smoke issuing trona one of the bedroom windows of a hods° occupied. by Mr.Connor,who is in the service of Messrs. Hesketh and Dutton. He went into the house, proceeded upstairs,and found one of the bed- rooms 80 full of smoke that if he had not quickly opened the window ha would have been suffocated. It was subsequently found that a boy had struck a match and thrown it on some clothes which wera commencing to blaze, but Superintendent Turner, assisted by two other firemen who had been sent for, soon put out the flames. It is believed that if the fire had not been discovered so promptly it would have been of a serious character.

The Late Mr. T. G. Rylands.

At three o'clock on Saturday afternoon, the e- mains of the late Mr. Thomas Glazebrook Rylands were cremated at the Manchester Crematorium, Chorlten-cum-Hardy. The funeral cortege left de- ceased's late residence, Highfield, Thelwall, shortly before one o'clock and proceeded by the 1.23 train to Manchester. The service at the Crematorium was conducted by the Rev T Pym Williamsou,vicar of Thelwall. The chief mourners were Messrs J P Rylands and W H Rylands (sons of the deceased). lt P 11 Rylands, L Gordon Rylands, W P Rylands, F K Glazabrook, W H Bleckly, J J Ble.ckly, W Long.R G Henshall, J C Bromfield, Rev George Fdather and 1 others. Many handsome floral tributes were seat, including wreaths from the widow and daughter, Lady Sowler,Mr G R Crosfield, Mrs TT obson (Wigan), the Misses Ashlin (Claughton), Mr W CrAnpton Ashlin, the grandchildren at Charle4ville, Btrken- head, and the Rev G and Mrs Feather, Glaze- bury. The coffin was made of oak. hand- somely panelled, but devoid of any mounting or breast plate. the funeral arrangemants were satisfactorily carried out, by Mr. Ralph Johnson. On Friday evening last week a Smoking Concert was held in the Reading-reom of the iberal Club the chair being occupied by Mr J Worrell, The Chairmen in a few well chosen remarks fon )wing on Mr W Critchley's song" Volunteers," said he wished to call for volunteers, but voluntcey of a different kind. These concerts entailed a lot of extra work on Mr Lamb, their manager, and he would like two or three to give a little assistance. Mr T lieetem, Mr J Davies and Mr E Llodgkinson at once offered their services and rendeied great help by tie way in which they attended to the requirements of the gentlemen present.—Mr T Horrocks, of Appley Bridge, the possessor of a fine baritone voice fairly brought down the house by he way in which he rendered his three songs viz :—" The Skipper," "Father O'Flynn," and "Soldiers of the Queen."— Mr Clarke and Mr Price caused great umu3ement by their comic songs the former giving "Curiosity" and. " A pretty little place inside," the latter " Beauti- ful" "Stand up " and "Too hard," Mr W Whit- taker gave one of his whistling solos. Messrs W Peyton, Mus. Bac., and R H Peareen qere a duet on the piano and violin entitled "Sign de Bade." Mr W Woods sang "The King's Own," Mr Gandy, a parody on" Where are you going to my pretty maid," Mr L Lea" Let me like a Soldier fall," Mr C Warren, "Sweet Genevieve," Mr B A Sanders gave "A sketch on Physiognomy." /r W Critcbley Rave another song and a vote of thanks to the Chairman was moved by Mr W Ford. The Chairman after having replied thanked all performers who had taken part in the concert, especially Messrs Payton and Pearson for their duet, and Messrs Horrocks and Clarke for their songs. A most enjoyable con- cert, which was very well attended, was brought to a close by the singing of" God save tbe Queen."

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
Half-yearly Meeting. Lively proceedings.

The half-yearly meeting of the sharehoiders of the Kinelicster Ship Canal Company was held on Wednes- day morning, in the Association Hall, Manchester, Mr. J. K. Bythell, chairman of directors, presiding over a large attendance. The Chairman in moving the adoption of the report. said that luoking at the work of the past half-year, they saw undoubtedly much

ROOM FOR ENCOURAGEMENT although circumstances that were quite unforeseen and entirely beyond the control of the directors had pre- vented the result from coming up to the reasonable estimate of the directors. If they looked at the work of the whole year, there was even more ground for hope- fulness. He had told them more than once that their great undertaking could never be a great success until they had a great shipowning community in Macebester (Hear, hear.) Appreciating that fact, their greatest effort had been the formation of a local steamship com- pany callei the Manchester Liners. They did not expect any immediate development, but they had good reason to believe that their revenue last year would be very largely benefited, especially during the last half-year. It was the hope that the advent of the Manchester Liners was only ths forerunner of that great shipowning busi- ness without which their per: could never be made great (Applause.) It was a most extraordinary thing that, although something like 150 steamers had been calla] upon by the Government for transport purposes,and sailings from American ports had consequently dimietisheJ, up Cu recently the

- FREIGHTS HAD BEEN EXTREMELY LOW, and not mucla more than to cover expenses on the pre- sent high price of coal and other materials. That was mainly o ming to the cotton crop in America being kept back for some reason, shipments being abnormally small. A large increase of the shipments to this country had been diverted to Manchester. The imports of cotton to Manchester during the four months referred to had, however, only been 114,000 bales, against 145,000 bales the prev:ous year. On the other hand, they were fortu- nate in having increased imperts of Eeyntian cotton, re- ceiving 55,000 bales, as against 33,000 for the same period of las; year; and as Egyptian bales were much heavier than American blies, the practical result was that they had no falling off on the whole, though they had no increase to record. Up to the pre- sent time the percentage of shipments so far made to Manchester were 17 per cent. of the whole, whereas up to the same day last year they had only had 10 per cent, of the whole. The shipments from Alexandria.up to the end of last week, ...ero 99,000 bales, against 53,000 bales. Consequently heil.z,ellght they were justified in looking for a considerable increteee. on the whole seeson. Liverpool had also suffered, and the relative results at the two ports justified him in saying that there were many reasons for encouragement. They had to remember that they were eemnaring with a very good half year. The last half of 1898, compared with the last half of 1897,showed an increase on revenue of £22,200, and that was what they were comparing with now. The increase in the receipts of the last half year of 1897 as compared with 1896 was only £6220. This half-year they had an increase of £ll,OBO. On seaborne traffic they had aa increase of ewer 99,211 tons, notwithstanding that they had a dearease of 46,000 tons of coal. Further if they compared the year 1894—the year the canal was opened —with 1899 they found that, whereas in 1894 they bad 686,000 tons of seaborne merchandise, they had last year 2,420,000 tens. (Hear, hear.) If they included Bridge %racer traffic, they couli compare the figures thus- -926,000 tons in 1894, 2,278.000 tons in 1899. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately, besides the diffieulty he had referred to with regard to vhssels being diverted to the service of the Government, and in addition to the failute of the cotton crop, they had to face difficulties which affected their not revenue. Difficul- ties quite unexpected and quito beyond control. They had had a timber trade of 280,000 tons, as against 213,000 tons during the past year, and tley meet have more room fer deck accommodation. If the shareholders did not provide it they had better shut the port UP. (Applause.) Taking the half-year ending June, 1897, their 'Tempts were £97,330, and their expenditure £98,228, leaving a werking loss of £894. Taking the half-y ear just terminated, the receipts were £140,592, and their expenditure £99,807, leaving a working profit of £10,807. Tlur 4towed that whilst the increased re- ceipts were 243,262, the increased expenditure was only £1,583, in epite of the difficulties they had had to con- tend against. (Applause.)

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Message from Lord Roberts. Boers Scattered in all Directions. A Kopje and Fifty Prisoners Taken. Boers Just Arrived from Ladysmith The following was ye3taday pasted at the War Office :

From Lord Roberts to the Secretary of State f^r War Paardeberg, February 21 (delay( d in transmission).— Yesterday afternoon I was satisfied by a careful recon naisgance in force of the enemy's position that I could not assault it without a very heavy loss, which I was most anxious to avoid. Accordingly I decided to bombard him with artillery and to turn my attention to the enemy's reinforcements. The result was most satisfactory. The Boers were driven off in all directions, lazing a good many killed and wounded ,and about fifty prisoners who state that they arrived from Ladysmith two days ago by railway. They say that it was our artillery fire which caused them to abandon tbe kopja they were occupying. Our loss consisted of two offimrs—Captain Campbell, 9th Lancers, and Lieutenant Houston, Royal Horse Artillery—and four men, all slightly wounded. CRONJE AT BAY.
A Cosfly Fight. The Boers Lose Heavily. The Enemy Surrounded. PAARDEBERG. FEBRUARY 20.
The fight is ow of the most c,ostly of the war. Kelly Kenny advanced to Boer la?.ger at Blip Drift, and action began ac; daybreak mounted infantry driving
in enemy's rearguard. Our main body was on the north side of the river, moving to outflank the laagers. Kelly-Kenny seized both drifts, and ordered the attaek, finding enemy enclosed.
In the attack the Highland Brigade was on the left and Knox's Brigade in the centre.

The ground was level on both banks,and the advance was deadly. The Boers confess to a loss of over 800. On Monday we opened fire from 50 guns. A later message says tho British captured one kopje and took 50 prisoners.
Attempt to Relieve Oronje
by Botha.
Boer Commando Scattered.

The London" Evening Nows " correvpandent tele- graphing from Pdardeberg, February 21 (4.50 p.m.) says : Commandant B)tha is attmopting zo relieve Cronjo. There has been severe fighting, and hie commando is scattered. They lost heavily.
Cronje Asks for an Armistice.
DIODDEFL RIVER (WEDNESDAY I)), 10 P.M.
General Kelly-Kmny's division was engaged through- out Sunday and Monday in a vigorous attack upon General Cronje's form., which was in laager on the north bank of the Modder River.
The Boers offered a most stubborn resistance despite an admittedly heavy loss,and on Tuesday General Cronja asked for an armistice.
Another Runcorn Man for The Front.

Private George Shone,the Ist V.B. Cheshire Regiment, and on of the lAto Mr. Gelrge Stone, of the George and Dragon Hotel, Runcern, has sailed 'with the contingent of Cbeahiro Voluuteers, for active service in South Africa.

div.head: Swelling the Runcorn War Fund.
div.p: Swelling the Runcorn War Fund.
The Runcorn Volunteer Band attended the football match between Runcorn and St. Helens last Saturday, and realised about £4. as the result of a callection,which will be devoted to the local war fund.

div.head: Widnes Volunteers.—Enthusiastic
div.p: The Widnes Volunteers.—Enthusiastic
Farewell.

The send-off to the gallant young fellows who have volunteered for active service in South Africa from Widnes took place on Tuesday night. The initial part of the send-eff was the entertainment at dinner of the contingent by Mr. George Ingram Neil (the Mayor) at Law's Commercial Hotel. There were present the Mayor (Mr. Neil), Major Lewis (of the Widnes Volunteers), Captain Sayco (2nd Lancasuire Volunteer Engineers), Dr McLennon, Mr. Hoyle, Mr. Craik, Mr. Charles Lewis, Mr. Joseph Pritchard, and Mr. Horner. The Widnes con- tingent numbered eleven men and two officers (Lieuten- ants Lewis and 11)hinson). After the dinner,the Mayor proposed "The Queen." This was drunk heartily with musical honours. The next toast was that of " The Army, Navy, and Auxiliary Farces," proposed by Mr. Horner, to which Major Lewis responded. The remain- der of the meetin,4 was ;pent in a convivial manner,acd several presentaticns were made to the officers and men. The men had a hear 'T send-oN at the station by large crowds of s2cctators, accompanied by two bands of the town.

Concert at Widnes. On Monday twning a concert, promoted by the Widgel Relief Ftlad Cconarnittee, was held in the Drill Vail. Over tlstS entrance to the buildin2 appoved gag jets framing the word!!, " 001 Ba-a the Queen," whilst the national dig floated frroin a flagstaff. There was a crowded audience, including the Mayor (Alderman G I Nail), Alderman Wareing, Councillors Christie, Laws 9 S 'th Bulla ugh9 Shuttleworth, &c. The programme , dr was an excellent one. It opened with the selection, -A. " Gems of Victorian 'by tin Widnes Subscrip- tion Band. Then folliewed the piece " The Area Belle," t by the Farnworth Musical and Dramatic Society. The characters were taken as follows :—Pitcher, Mr W Norris Jones ; Tosser, Mr J Pritchard ; Walker-Chalks, Mr J Timmins ; Penelope, Mrs W NJrris-Jones; and Mrs Crocker, Mrs J 11111Milnl. The sketch was well enacted. Mr A J Squires was stage manager. The second por- tion of the programme consisted of songs, glees, &c. At the conclusion a vas of thanks was accordei to the artistes for their lerv;ces, and Co the gentlemen who had lent the articl,s, &c., meationod above. I is expected that the war fund will be materially augmented by the proceeds.

div.head: More Earlestown Volunteers for the Front. .
div.p: More Earlestown Volunteers for the Front. .

Earlestown was early astir on Monday morning to witness the departure of three more Volunteers for active service at the front—namely, Messrs. Booth, Shallcross, and Dean. None of the men have had any experience in military matters, but notwithstanling this they gallantly offered their services and were accepted. Two of the number are members of St. John's Bible Class and the superintendent, Mr Thomas Molynsux, taking a great interest in their departure, considerately secured the services of the Earlatown Prize Band. A procession was formed on the Market-square, the members of the Bible Class leading. The band on their way played "Soldiers of tt:e Qheen "and the National Anthem, and a crowd of 500 sang the refrains with great enthusiasm. Arriving at the 9tatioa, various patriotic airs were ren- dered until the time of. the dep xrture of the train for War- rington, which left at seven o'clock,amid much cheering and the singing of" Auld Lang Sync." The aim, who were in khaki, will probably be placed in the ranka of the Ist South Lancashire R^giment.

" Send-off " to An Orford Volunteer. The frietAds of Mr. Fred Woods (No. 7,126), who left Warrington for the front with the Warrington conting cut of the South Lancashire Feetion of Volunteers met at the Longford Hotel on Saturday evening for the pu-- pose of giving him a hearty "send-off." A good supper was supplied by the landlord, Mr. Hatton, after which t, an entertainment was provided under the superinten- dence of the secretary Mr. John Povey,and a committee. Mr. A.C. Binks was elected to the chair,and Mr. Thomp- son to the vice-chair. A presentation cons:sting of a smoking outfit and a pure of money was then made to Mr. Woods on behalf of his friends, by the Chairman. Mr. Fred Woods suitably responded, and thanked the donors for the valuable preseLts. Other m.mbers of the Cunpany expressed their good wishes in a few and well- chosen remarks. A vote of thanks to the chairmon,and the singing of the National Anthem and " Au:d Lang Syne " concluded the proceedings.

div.head: DEPARTURE OF LOCAL VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: DEPARTURE OF LOCAL VOLUNTEERS.
ENTHUSIASTIC "SEND-OFF."
Memorable Scenes at Warrington.

Warrington has been in a state of patriotic fer- vour during the past week. Never before has so much enthusiasm prevailed, and it is probable that the event wilier) prompted it will not again occur in the lifetime of those who participated in it. The occasion was tne departure for South Africa of the contingent of Warrington Volunteers who are to reinforce the South Lancashire Regiment which at this moment is near Ladysmith. The parting fare- well did not take place until Thursday midnight, but the moit important functions in connection with the " send-off " were a parting service in the Parish Church and the public dinner in the Parr Hall, on Monday evening. The service was originally intended to be held on the previous Sunday but at the suggestion of several Nonconformists who were desirous of attending, the Rector decided to hold a week-night service. And a most successful and impressive service it was. The "old church" as it is still called was filled to overflowing. Every seat allotted to the public was filled long before the time fixed for the service to commence.

The Mayor had arranged to leave the Town Hall at 5,30 to walk in procession to the Parish Church accompanied by the South African contingent of Volunteers and the members of the Corporation. Very few of the latter, however, put in an appear- ance, and the procession was not as strong as it has been on many an occasion lately. Darkness was creeping on as the 68 chosen representatives of the Warrington Volunteer Battalion paraded in front of the Town Hall in commaud of Captain Appleton. The people cheered them,and well they might, for a finer set of men it would be difficult to find. Their stay at the Baraacks had greatly improved their physique. Tney had the bearing of well- trained soldiers and underlying their snuff-coloured suits of khaki there was the bone and muscle of well-developed men. They were in every way worthy successors of the men who nearly one hun- dred years ago in the hour of their country's need gallantly came forward and formed themselves into a corps which is still lanwn as the loyal Bluebacks. That same patriotic spirit which was then witnessed is with us to-day, and while it lasts, the spectre of conscription will remain in the background. At the appointed time, the picturesque figures of the sword and mace bearers might have been seen descending the steps of the Town Hall. They were followed by the Mayor bedecked with his gown and chain of office. Immediately, the order was given to the Volunteers to march and at a swinging pace they proceeded down the eastern avenue where they were met by the Volunteer band and a posse of police. The whole moved cif to the accom- paniment of a lively tune, but the progress of the processionists was somewhat retarded by the press of the people who were desirous of getting a peep at our local knights in khaki. The toll of the Parish Church bells could be heard as the procession neared the sacred pile‘with its spire standing out dimly ia the gathering darkness. There was a clash of music as the strains of the band commingled with the steady tolling of the bells. Suddenly both ceased, and in a moment the clergy and choir in their vestments appeared at the door to meet the civic procession. The Volunteers lined up from the gates to the church door and afterwards brought up the rear. As they took the seats which had been reserved for them they were the cynosure of all eyes. The service was one well-calculated to befit the men for the fiery ordeal on which they are about to enter. At the close, the Rector very thoughtfully presented each Volunteer with an embossed card with the colours of the regiment and bearing a suitable prayer. Very different indeed was the character of the proceedings afterwards conducted in Parr Hall. Where there had been impressiveness and solemnity at the Parish Church there was now enthusiasm and gaiety. The festive board was elaborately set out and the guests were waited upon by Volun- teers whose bright uniforms relieved the more sombre coloured suits of the diners. The Procession.

The Volunteers arrived from the Barracks at the Town Hall, at about 5 30 and were greeted with hearty cheers. They were attired in their lzhaki uniform, and looked very smart and trim, their soldierly appearance being freely commented upon. Captain Appleton was in command, and the men were drawn up in double rank facing the Hall. A processim was at nnce formed beaded by the Volunteer band under the direction of Bandmaster T. Armstrong. "The gentlemen in Khaki' came next,followed by a tiff of police,with whom were Chief-Inspector Phillips and Inspector Taylor. Then came the Mayor (Alderman Robsrts),liho was accompanied by his Chaplin (the Rev. John Yonge), and the Town Clerk (Mr. J Lyon Whittle), followed by Lieutenant-Colonel filway, Major Buckton, and Cap'ain Hutchinson, V.D., the members of the Town Council, the officials, and a number of prominent townsmen. Hundreds of people lined the route to the ct urch, and the Service men were vociferously cheered. From several of the houses and shops flags were displayed, and every pint of vantage for viewing the procession wag sseured. • At the Parish Church,

j An exceedingly lame congregation had assembled at the Parish Church. The precession was met at the dear !by the clergy and the members of the choir and the score, as the 'Volunteers entered the sacred edifice was a j most impressive one. The whole of the congregation stood until they hal teken their seats, the organist Mr. . Woods, playing a voiuntary. Amengst the clergy present were the Revs. Canon Willis (Rector), E J Will- cocke (headmaster of the Grammar School), I S Cameron and A F White (curates), J Davies (vicar of St. A.nn's),Ei V Pigot (vicar of St. Thomas's Stockton Hes.th) F E Poweil (vic a of St. Janrs's, Latchford,) and E R Tartu* (vicar ef St. Paul's). The service was con- ducted by the Rector assisted by the Revs. A F White, A S Cane-o', J D :vie!, and H V Pigor. Special colleet2 we rvel aud r. ealin xlvi. commenc- ing "God is our hope arid o:wngth" was sung. The singing of the hymns" Eloly father in Thy msrcy," " 0 God our help in ages pest." and "Abide with me," was accsmpaeied by the Volenteer Band. The Recter preached an apteropriate eermon from the words" The Lord bleu thee and keep thee. The Lord make His faco shine upon and be graeions unto thee. The Lord lift up his couatenance upon thee and give thee peace." Book of Numbers, vi. 24, 25, 26. Daring the course of his remarks he said he had to thank publicly the Noncen- formist ministers for the suggestion of that week nigh!., service. It was owing to them that the service was held that night. Centinuing ke said, he would point them to the present poeition of affairs in South Africa. For the last four months they had heard of nothing but reverses and he thought, if one might say so, it had added to their eeteem of the English people that those reverses had been borne as they had, hue within the last day or two their hearts had been cheered by clad news of success, for which God be thanked and God be praieed. With regard to their Qireen and their country,the British Empire, they knew what they all owed to their country. It was God who had given us that great inheritance, the British Empire. Surely it was not to be lightly thrown j away. They wore to fight for their Queen and for their . country and for this glorious Empire. And why ? Beeatrie it was for the honour and glory of God that the great gospel of Jesus Christ might be spreed by English- men throughout the world. This VC2.3 what commended the war to his heart, sad as it is. It was he bslieved under Gal for the good of men aed for the honour and glory of God. And so he could dismiss them now, con- cluded the Rector, with that beautiful blessine " The Lord bless thee and keep thee. The Lord make his face to rhino upon thee and be gracious unto thee. The Lord lift up his countenance upon thee and eive thee peace. At the conclusion of the service the National Anthem was snag and each voluetetir was pretented with a prayer card, on which WAS a photeeraph of the Queen and the crest and colours of the Volunteer Regiment. The prayer which had been prepared b.e the Rector as j Cnaplain of the Corps read as &Wows :—A daily prayer ' for the Volunteers of the South Lancashire Regiin, et while serving in Africa. Our Father . . . Amen. 0 Lord God of Hosts, Who hast called me to take part in this war in the service of my Queen and country, help me to be faithful in the performance of my duty, patient and cheerful under all trials, fearless in danger, merciful in success. If it please Thee, grant victory to our arms. Make me a good soldier of Jesus Cfn4s'3, never ashamed of my religion, and prepared at any time if deed be to die. Keep under Thy protecting care all my dear re- lations and friends, especially . . . . and if it be Ehy gracious will, hrirJE,, me back in health and safety to my home. Grant this, I beseech Thee, for Jesus Christ's sake Amen.

During dinner, the Volunteer Band played some mactial mutic and Mr. Randall also gave several s.lec- tions on the orzan. The guests were waited up ln by volunteers, and their scarlet uniforms heightened the effectiveness of the scene.
Letters of Apology. Opinions of Absentees.

Letters apologizing for inability to be present had been received from the following gentlemen :—Mr:James Hepherd,lLieutenant A Northern (Orford Barracks), Mr John White, Mr William Long. Mr %V D Jeene, sen., Mr F L Bennie, Mr W S Howard, Councillor Shillcock, Mr R Young (cemetery registrae),aud the Rev Father Po'dine. Mr. F. Monks wrote from Bournemouth West. My dear Mr. Mayor : lam sorry I cannot be with you on Monday at the dinner to the Volunteers who are going out to South Africa. They have our hearty good wishes for a safe return from duties that will try their patience, skill, and fortitude. They are going out in defence of the liberties of our people, and though it is two of our colonies that are attacked the blow is felt by all of us, and we respond to the challenge in the same spirit that our forefathers have done in the pas:. This is no war of conquest, but one which has been forced upon 13 by the men who owe their own lives to the pro- tecting arm of our own countrymen. We have met with checks and reverses, but these have only shown the bravery of our men, and the splendid courage with which they have done more than hold their own against overwhelming odds. We all rejoice in the relief of Kim- berley, and hops very soon to do tho same for Lady- smith and Mafeking, but the great task of freeing South Africa from the tyranny and corruption of the Repub- lics and the pelitical ideals of the B )ers remains to be accomplished, and to assist in this we wish our Volun- teen " God speed the right." One result of teis war will be to bring the importance and value of our Volun- teers as a defensive force into greater prominence, and secure for them greater encouragement and financiil assistance from the Government. The reform of our War Office and its administration will come in due time, but our present duty is to support every eff )rt that make for the unity and strecigtn of the Empire, and to give all moral and material support t 3 those upon whom :he burden of the struggle mainly rests. I join most he trtily with you and my fellow-townsmen in the send- off to our Volunteers in the full confidence that they will bar themselves like men in the defence of right and love of country. Yours faithfully, F. Mosxs. Colonel Spearr regretted tnat absence in the South of England on Monday next, owing to the serious illness of a very near relative, prevented his accepting the kind invitation of the Mayor of Warrington to the dinner given to the Volunteers of the let B. Y.W.V. South Len. cashire Regiment who have accepted service lathe war In South Africa. _ _ _

The Rev. E. T. REED wrote :—To his Worabip the Mayor of Warrington. Dear Mr. Meyer,—! beg to acknowledge the receipt of your circular letter of yester- day's date, inviting an to a public dinner on Monday evenin,,, next, in connection with the departure of the local Volunteers for South Africa. Ic wouki have given me pleasure to accept your kind invitation had I been able conscLntiously to do so ; but after a 9 carefol 3T I thorough a study of the causes which lcd to the out- break of hostilli3s as I have been able to devote to the subject, I have not as yet found myself at lib4rty to depart from the position taken by Sir Edward Clarke, in October last, viz:— " That this lamentable war on which we are embarked is an absolut,ly unnecessary war." This being my opinion I feel that I cannot countenance by my prvonce any proceedings in the direction of the carrying on of the war, nor do I believe in the policy of " seeing it through"; for it seems to me our Government ought to definitely state to the Transvaal G)vernment what it is we are fighting f&or,b7fore procceJing with a sanguinary campaigh the duration and expense of which no ori,!! can tell. For the men who are going out I feel great sTm- pathy because in all probability they will encounter both suffering and death in what I conceive to be an ingl)ri• ous cau9e. There is another. reason why I cannot sre my way to accept yoar kind invitation, viz :—That while so many millions of oar fellow subjects in India are starving or on the vary of starvatbn I feel that any money I have to spare should be given to help them Air- ing this time of unparalleled scarcity and dire distress in our Indian Empire. You will I am sur, receive this letter as a statement of my personal views upon the gravest moral crisis through which as a nation we have been called to pass during my r.wa acd you wilt also believe me when I sty that in all public matters in which I can conscientiously take part it will be a 11-a! pleasure to me to give you my ungrudging and hearty support.—Believe me to remain, dear Mr. Mayor, sin- cerely yours, EDWARD T. REED.

No furtksr words of his were needed to commend the toast to their acc?ptance. (Hear. hear.) Toe RECT')E, in r-sponding. said he hid great pride in doing ,o, however unwortniiy. He wished their own olci li.hop (Dr. Ryla) had b able to be with them that evenbg. Ile would have asked him to have a.tided chw service and given them his hessiug. It was his earaeit desire to die in harnen, bit a hen a man was 81 years of ae ho p):haps felt that it b weil for the Caurch and tho people to re;ign his office. On; hi; was a mail wh hid done eis duty in his day. (1p- : lie was a very good old man, aid they were all sorry to los him. He expressed in his aldress his appreciation of the kindness of the Nonconformist in;nisters, to whom they owed the very beautiful service that had been be:d_that evening in the Parish Church.

Trio Rev. Jones YONGE also respandel, aril said on behalf of the ministers of the Nuneonfortnist Caurches of Warrington, he bagged to Leader their very cordial thanks. This was one of those occasions in which men of all creeds, sects and parties, and eyrie men who did not belong to any sect, creed or party, could cordiAlly and harmoniously unite. They had met together that evening as citizene, not only of the good old town of Warrington, but of the United Kingdom(applause)and they 'nad met for the expres parpese of assuring their to emsmen who were going out to the war of their cur ial sympathy and earnest goodwill. He might say on behalf of thse he might be suppssed to represent that he cordially and thoroughly appreciated the spirt of patriotism which had moved these men to offer their services to their country, (Hear, hear, and ppLuse.) Ile was s ire that all present would agree with him when he said that the widespread willoigness throughout the country of loyal Britons to come to the help of the country in her dine of need was a magnificent thing; and he would venture to say one thing more, and that was that it was his belief that while that spirit lasted— and he believed it avould last—they need not be afraid of anything else than voluntaryism in connection with the miltary forces of this country. (Lou,' applause.) Might he also be permitted to add one other sentence ? and that was that the fNoncanformists of the country were as !opal and as patriotic as any other classes in the kingdom. (Hear, hear, and applause.) It might be that some of them were not particularly enamoured of the new Imperialism, but he begged to assure the audi- ence %It they were not little Englanders. (Applause.) They loved their country,they bored and reverenced their Quern, they were proud of her military and naval defenders, and they longed to have the grand old cone- try, in which they had been born, respected and hon- oured by all the nations of the earth. (Applause.) They wished that night their fellow townsmen " God-speed " and success in their efforts, and if it pleased a merci- ful Providence, a safe return to their homes. (Ap- plause.)

The MAYOR, stepping to the front of the platform, stated that a short time ag) he made an appeal to the people of Warrington to as2ist him in making a suitable presentation, in recognition of the patriotism of the men who; were leaving Warrington for the front. That res- ponse had been so satisfactory that he was able on his own behalf, and on theirs' to present to Captain Appleton and each of ilia men a field glass and a lifo policy for £lOO. (Applause.) Captain APPLETON was the first to step forward,and he was greeted with loud and hearty cheers. The Mayor then presented him with a field glass enclosed in a leather case (with straps attached.) The case bears the following inssription :—"To Captain F M Appletrm, lit Volunteer Battalion Prince of Wales's Volunteers. South Lancashire Regiment, from the Mayor and townspeople of Warring- ton as a memento of their warm appreciation of his patriotism in volunteering for active service in the war in South Africa, 1900." All the men responded to their names as they were called out by Adjutant Major Roome.

div.head: TOASTS.
div.p: THE TOASTS.
"The Queen."

The first teast of the evening was that of the Queen. The MAYOR 9 kid that on occasions liko Ui se it WAR the proud privilege of Enzlishmen to drink to the health of their Sovereign. Our na;:ion had every ',won to be deeply thankl'ul that it had had at the head of affai's for an unparalleled period a monarch whose womanly sweetness, intense sympathy with all in sorrew and dis- tress, and whose purity of life and condu3t had won for her the reverent affection of all her pe0p1..% hear.) They deeply regretted that to the burden of her vsnerable years should be added the sadness cmseqkunt on the present war ; hut if ansthiag could possibly aui to the unbounded affection with which they regarded her it would be the fortitude she had shown in her pre- sent trials and the tenderness with which she had so often endemxsured to mitigate the grief of those sorely stricken. When the Queen's supremacy had been re- established in South Africa. and the blessings Gf peace again pr,vaileci—and he prayed God that might be very speedily accomplished—might their bel,wed Sovereign live to see the foundations of her vast Empire further strengthened and consolidated by the ever-increasiJg patriotina of her subj•icts. (Applause.) The to.a3t was drunk with musical honours.

"The Prince and Princess and Royal Family," The MAYon s aid he had another toast to submit, and one which, he felt sure, w uld find a most ready and cordial acceptance at their bands, and that was" His Royal Flighness the Prince of Wales, the Princess oF. wa!es,and the rest of the Royal Family." (Applause.) With regard to the Prince. Ire was a worthy son of a worthy mother. He had seen him renerilly deacril3el as " The fint gentleman of Earep !," and he believed it. (Applause.) But if that was true of him, :ind they knew it was, what should he say of his most excellent wife ? If the Prince was the first gentleman in Europe the Princess was par excellence the first lady in Europe. (Applause.) As for the rest of the Royal Family they were a down-right good sort. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with music 41 hoooor3 and the singing of "God bless the Princl of Wales."
"The Bishops and Clergy and all Ministers of Religion,"

Councillor MONKS in proposing this to is said he took it that tlie princip3l obj.!ct of the meeting was to expresq their admiration of the manner ia which some of the Volunteers had come forward at the call of duty to servo the Queen in South Africa. Just ac they admired three men for the promptur.ss with whlch they had cmne for- ward, in the same way they aPpre.-...iatd the hard work and psinstak:ng duties which the biahops, clergy, and au i ininisZ,ors of relit; (3u s!-,owed cv.,ry day of thE..i:
Mr. Pierpoint and the Army and Navy. -

Mr. R. PIEEtPOINT, M.P. proposed the toast of "The Navy. Army, and Reserve Forces." He thought on an oczaaion like;that he might almost have hid placed in his hands the toast with the simple words" The Army and Navy," because tc-day the army was so intimately knit with auxiliary farces, particularly our military farces, that it might new be considered as one army. Of the navy he need say but a very little. They all knew its value. They all knew that it was the biggest, and the finest navy in the world, and the finest navy the world had ever produced. But fine as it was he hoped thet now it rhight be made finer and bigger still. (dear, hear.) Toe navy, so far as the ships were concerned had had no opportunity of carrying an any part of the war, but the officers and the Bluejackets had done admirable service, indeed. Had it not been for the cervices of the naval officers and of the Bluejackets, Ladysmith which was making such a glorious defence would scarcely have been able to hold out. (Applause.) They were very proud of this army of theirseland War- rington was setting a very good example to the arme and to the country at large. (Hear, hear.) He might say it a 4 a Warrington man—and he was sure they would all endorse what he said—that they were exceed- ingly proud of what oer Warrington men were doing to- day. (Applause.) He might perhaps, be allowed, to add, witnont takiag too rnuch upon himself, and seem- ing to assume a vanity, that those who had served as he did, unfortunately in the years long gone by, in this corps, of which they were all so proud, that he felt some special pride ie the fax', that he might call himeel cc honorary memter of the corps, and might take the liberty of calling teem "my comrades." (Applause.) They would watch the men who were going out with interest, and trusted that God's providence might watch over them and Captain Appleton. (Applause.) They ' were having a peaue time that night but he hoped they would have a prouder moment still on the day when they marched back into the good old town, and perfect in their conscience that they had done their duty to their I Q leen and country. (Applause.) He trusted that when the war was over it would no found possible to have a vary large ovorheuliag of our military arrangements— (hear. hear)—and especially of the office which controlled them. (Laughter and applause). He trusted that we were now seeing the begin- ning of the end, and that the end might come soon, with a glorious victory and a lasting peace. But before he sat down letehiat tell them of one lessen they had burr, day ey day, week by week, month by month, and that they would continue to learn as time went en—that our soldiers of to-day, the young fellows of to-lay, were worthy successors of the mon who fought under Welling:en in the Peninsular, of the men weo fought at Waterloo, of the men who fought in India and in the Crimea, and of the man who had fought our battles all over the world, and as long as we had such men to fiztit Our battles, England bad nothing to fear. (Cheers.)

div.head: Colonel Ridgway Appeals for Recruits.
div.p: Colonel Ridgway Appeals for Recruits.

Coloael RIDGWAY, raven:Hag said the army had won the empire, and it struck him that they as Englishmen were going to stick to it. In South Africa, what had been dons had beek. written large, and it would be written larger in the history of the war and of the country. Bet he sleet net forget the reserve forces. They had come uo :least nobly, and he was sure it mu t be vary pleasing far the officers of the line, who had had what was one of the fir6t serious experiments in calling up the reserves, to find that they had turned out so estiefacterily—men leaving heave family, work and good places to follow her Majesty's drum to fight for her 6,000 miles away. .Ngt a Man in the South Lanceshires at all events was =ping, and that was a proud thing to be able to say ;it was also a proud boast for English men to send oue to the world. (Applause,) We bad not been treated in the way in whith we had treated others. When France and Germany Were locked in a deadly struggle what did we do? We did not send 1 oat cartoons to insult the Emperor of the French or the Emperor and Eneprehs of Germany, but Z 500,000 to aisist their wounded. ;Applause.) They would let , r that peee,altheuele they would remember it. They would 'not be spiteful, bat be Englishmen—true to their Queea and country. Speaking of the navy,he was reminded that they all loved Jack, particularly the girls. (Laughter.) Speaking of the marines he said perhaps it mieht be thought by some that the marines had not dine much. He was reminded. that last week, in ehowing the losses of our tro3p3 in South Africa, it was reported that a marine detechtnent, with a body of troops—only same 200 jrnen---yet out of that body 78 ware eiteser killed, woanded, or rnlssiag. They had shown the ruff they were made of ; so had every battalion that had come uo and volunteered for the front, ana he was sure that when the men got out they would do their duty as Englishmen. (Applause.) Now he bad to speak of the force he represented, namely, the Volunteers. What they had done had been an experiment. Hitherto their motto had been " Defence, not defiance." What had they done? They had taken out the " not" and POW ealieel it " Defence, defiance "—(hear, hear)—but whole her elajisty's realm was no longer in danger they would go back tc " Defenee, not defiance." However, as lone as her Majesty wanted far troops they would be ready he trusted, to defend her interests mai to go out, no matter where it might be, no matter where she might send them. The Public would now have an opportunity of seeing what their Volunteers were who were going to the front. He had looked the Warrington men over frem the creams of,tueir. heads to the heels of their boets,and he defied any man to say that they were not a well-set lot of fellows. (Rear, hear, and applause.) They had the bone and sinew of Englishmen, and of the men of Lan- cashire too ; and he felt sure that they would go out with the hollow of the batlalion in their hands as well as the boaqnr of the South Lancashires. He trusted that ,as the Meinboe had remarked, they might safely return to Warringten, heit be felt sure that it would be with honeur. (Applause.) He now wished to do a little re- eruitieg. (Laughter.) He would tall them what he wanted. Thev were going to raise the battalion to 800, if peetible 1,000 (Applause.) He waeterl another 100 or 200 men, There were many men in Warrington :eh had plenty of time Si their dispesal, and he asked them to Coma forward and show themselves to be Englishmen, imitating those young fellows before them who were going to the front. Be would not ask them to undertake active service, but to make themeelyee useful to the country by drill and attention to duty. Mr. Pierpeint had said that there would be a great change in the mater of their arrange- ments, and he trusted that that would be the case. The Governm•nt had got everythine, they had the ball at t leir feet, ad all they had to do was to put forward a arrangemnat by which the yensible forces of the country could be put on a proper footing. The Volunteers were not put on a proper footing. What was wanted was dis- cipline and law, and he was sure that ever volunteer would say that ha felt a better man that day than he had ever dm° before. Be was healthy, and had good feod,and he learnt how to do his duty as a British soldier should do it. They wanted their men put On a proper footing to assist the Q iesn when the country , wan in danger, and he wished them to strengthen the hands of the Member RO that he could say to the Mims- try "You must do more for the Volunteers and draw the refine of discipline tighter." Discipline was certainly a rinA thing It made better men of all of them. They all had it in their school days, but after leaving school they foreot it to a great extent. In conclusion he wished to thank the Mayor and others for the kind man- ner in which the V -eunteers had blen entertained that evening, as the meetiee would he one of those pleasant memoriee they would clever forget,and when they got to

div.head: Warrington's Patriotic Sons.
div.p: Warrington's Patriotic Sons.

In proposing the toast of " Warrington'e Patriotic Sons" the aleeort said that when a few days ago he had the honour to attest the last ten of our local Volunteers, he ventured to say that he thought the time would not be' long before they should see the turn in the tide of affairs in S iuth Africa. He believed that that turn in the tide bed come, and, perhaps, he might convey to them a piece of information given to him by a gentleman connected with the press, and, of ceurse, everything which was given to thorn from suca an official and authoritative source as that must be cerreet. (Laughter.) The information he had received was in explanation of Cronje'e sudden retreat. He was informed that morning that the ceu.aes of that sudden retreat was the receipt by Cronjo of a private teleeram from Dr. Leyds to the effect that Captain Appleton and 70 Warrington men—(loud laugater)— weuld ehartly be at the front, and that he hid better take ocitasion by the hand and make the most of his op- portunity of getting away. (Renewed laughter.) He was only serry teat Cronje did not wait a little bit longer in order that the full measure of his defeat might have been accomplished with the aid of Warrington's patriotic sons. (Applause.) Allusion had been made that night to the marvellous manner in wnich from ail parts of the earth sons of the greater Britain had rallied to the defence of the Queen's authority. Whet was the explanation ? The proudest beast of the men of the ancient Roman empire, the greatest empire of tla. aacitiet, days, was " lam a liornan citizen." Wherever the British flag had been planted it had made, in spil:o of our follies, and, if they liked, in spite of our sins and shortcomings, in the main it always made for truth, for righteousness and for freedom. (Applat.Pe.) It was because oar people all the world over were ab e to say well greater pride than ever the anoients said it "I am a British citizen," and chat was the feeling whica animated them and caused them to come trom far dis- tant homes to make it impessible for the Queen's authorty in the long run to be denied. Teat same citizenship had animeced our townsmen. He had said on ' maey occasions theO he was proud of the town of his birth, but there never was an occasion on 7, hide ho felt that spirit of pride as he did on that occasion. He was grateful to them for the manner in which they hai sup- ported every appeal he had made to them on behalf of our soldiers and he was grateful to Captain Appleton and the men under his command her the henour which they had reflected ou the good old town by standing out now and taking their fair share in defending our S overeign's authority in Seth Africa. But he would say this, that in spite of all that had been given utterance to in regard to our interests in this war, nothing could exceed the feeling of personal interest they would now take in it, because man who had worked long with them in private and public affairs would now be working with and lighting along with their comrades in South Africa to being about waat they would assuredly obtain before very long, namely, the absolute and, he believed, the perpetual re assertion of the Queen's authority over the whole of her do- I minions in that far distant land. (Cheers.) While he hoped their Inert would not escape without a khock or two, and that while he should like them to ste, and ho knew they would wish to see, active service, he hoped most earnestly that they height roturn te War- rington safe and sound, in order that they might show them, by the strength of feeling which would obtain, haw highly they admired the prtriotism which they had displayed, and how glad they would be to welcome them been) the good old lowa waich they ware non, leaving. (Applause). Tha toast was received with inu,ical honeurs, the audience singing " For theyiare jolly good fellow." Captain Appleton Replies.

Captain APPLICTON.W4O on rising to reply had a hearty reception, said he was proud to say that ha was a soldier that night,and as a soldier he knew that it was his duty to Fay Mao, but te try to do much. (Hear, hear.) But he felt, on behalf of his non-commissioned officers and men from Warrington that he could not sit down with- out teline them how much they felt for what Warring- ton tad doao for them. It seemed to him that the people of Warrington had been hiving a sort of race to S.de whether their hearts were tne largest or the Volunteers backs the broadest. (Laughter.) They had simply loaded them with all they could think of,to help them on their way to make them more effieient,naore comfortable and to help them to do their duty when they got to South Africa. He thasked them for the most beautiful pair ot field glaoies. Re knew they were the very best that could be obtained, and ha could not tell them how tighly he should value them. They would be invaluable in the country to which they were going. Speaking on behalf of the battalion, which he had left for a time, they were only doing what every officer was eatiag his heart out to do, and that was to go to the front. They were only doing what thousands of soldiers wore doing in South Africa, and what many oilers of their fellow-townsmen were ready to do if they got the opportunity. He was quite cognizant of the great responsibility that lay upon himself and those uuder his command. They were going forth from a battalion they were eorry to leave for a time, but they were going to the first battalion of the regiment to which they were all proud to belong. They were going out to a regiment which was commanded by one vvhese name WAS still a heusehold word in the battalion, Colonel J Mc:.;arthy O'Leary. And now they ever° members of the old "Fighting 40th "the colours of which he looked at every 1-noreing at the Barracks; and he trusted he might Ido no thing to disgrace thorn or the -nen I under him. They were going out to refire- sent good old . Warrington, of which they were so prautand which ha lso well treated them. What their fellow-towmmen had done for them had gone deep into their hearts, and if they were " elesent-minded teggare" their hearts were not absent minded. What they bad done fr them weuld, he know, help them when they were far away. (Applause.) And if they had the privilege of beine in the fiehting line they would hear the eclace9 of " Play up, Warrington." (Cheers.) Thee meant to play up too. (Hear, hear.) He hIA got men from Warrington whom he was proud to command. They were a good set of fellews, ad they had earned the approval, he believed, of Colonel Sprat and his officers at the Barracks. They had a good spirit in them and he believed it was their utmost wish to do their duty, and to be worthy ef the great honour which had b ten entrueted to them. He hoped they might be per- mitted to return to Warrington after having brought honour upon the town. (Beer, hear, and applause.) He sheuld like to thank all whe had assisted them. The list was too long to enumerate but he would ask his men to give three cheers to them all, which was the best way of expressing their gratitude to them for all they bed done for them. The men then gave three hearty cheers. The Entertainment. Handsome Collection for the War Fund.

During the evening an excellent entertainment was provided t y s2veral well-kaown artistes. The first item was the ever popular "Soldiers of the Queen" by Mr. Pears°. the audience joining in the chorus with spirit. A charming gipsy dance by the lady pupil teachers at People's College folio we] and the audience gave vent to ther appraval wit vigorous applauie. The performers were tastefully attired and carried tambourines. The

next, and perhaps the most popular item of the evening was "The absent - minded beggar " which was faultlessly given by fourteen boys from Pe pie's College. The audience took up the chorus, and at tie conclusion of the song a cAtection wo :nade by the young ladies with ttuir tambourines in ail of the War Fund, which the Mayor announced, realized the handsome amount of 221105. 5L Mr. NAson Jackson was a host in himself, and his humorous contributions were greatly appreciated. Miss Sutton was successful in her song, as was Mr. Peers Brisielow with a flute solo. The Aeolian glee party feelingly sang " Home sweet Hom' e " and Mr. Ireland gave an excel- lent interpretation Gf" Let me like a soldier fall." Mr. ‘l7. H. Payton and Mr. Percy Randall accompanied. The proceedings were brought to a close with the singing of "Auld Lang Syne " and the National Anthem •abcut 11.30.

div.head: On the Way to the Barracks.
div.p: On the Way to the Barracks.

The proceedings at the Hall over, the "heroes of the hour " were escorted to the Barracks by the Volunteer Band, a large crowd carrying torches and flags marching in front. The greatest enthusiasm prevailed, several of the Volunteers being carried shoulder high. An Old Volunteer's Appreciation.

Mr. Woods, grocer, Scotland-road. has presented each of the msn going out to South Africa with a bundle of six cigars and a box of matches, as a mirk of respect to them. Mr. Woods was a member of the corps in its earlier history.

The Rev. J, Yonge and the Rector. The Rev- J. Yonge writes as fellows :—Sir,—ln speak- ing hurriedly, as is inevitable on 811 Ch an occasion as the dinner at the Parr Sall, on Monday night, one is sure to forget something important that one meant to have said. Thus I unhappily omitted to make any reference to the Rector's very kind acceptance of a suggestion from some Nonconformist ministers concerning the farewell service for our Volunteers. With your permission, I should like to publicly acknowledge the ready kindness with which the Rector arranged for this service to ba hcid last evening rather than upon Sunday. As we have had recently two public municipal church occasions on Sunday, which tend rather to disturb the congrega- tions in all the places of worship in the town,and should not, therefore, be unduly frequent, it has been a happy expedient to have bad this most interesting valedictory service on a week evening. It is to be hoped that espec- ially our fellow-townsmen who are leaving us for patrio- tic duty in South Africa will retain helpful impressions from that service, such impressions,indeed,as must have been received by all who thoughtfully took part in it. —Yours, Icc.
JOHN YONGE. 19, Wilson Patten-street, February 20th.

div.head: Letter from Staff-Sergeant Buckley
div.p: Letter from Staff-Sergeant Buckley
The Mayor and the Ambulance Men.

The following letter bas been received y Captain Waring, Chief Superintendent of the Warrington Ambul. ance Corps :—February 19th, 1900. No. 516 Staff Ser- geant J. G. Buckley, St. John's Tavern, Sc. John's Gate Clerkenwell, Leaden, E.C. Dear Captain Waring.—l now write to let you know that we leave here on Wed- nesday for Aldershot, and on Thursday we go to Southampton for South Africa. I have all the Warring. ten men with me except Dimolow, who goes out on the Moseley. I have had great praise from the Chief, and he told me to day that I was a first-class staff sergeant. I shall have four sergeants under me. We have to get two suits pyjamas each, which means 7s. 61. each. I thiair, considering what we have done, that Warrington should pay this for us. There is great fuss about the Volunteeref but nothing about us, and we are under great expense hero although we are kept free, good meat and everything else. I, Longmore and Madd:cks, leave our wives and children unnrovided for• You must write at once, or leave it until I write; bu': I think that I shall have to wish you a good-bye now. Remember me t) Mr. Crosfield, Hulse, and Dr. Adams, and tell them that we are right away for the Cape. No more this time, from your "absent-minded beggar," J. S. Buckley. P.S.— Remember me to the lads,and tell them that Warrington is not behind.

The attention of the Mayor having been drawn to the fact that the members of the Ambulance Brigade re- quired furthnr equipment, his Worship sent by telegram tne sum of £6 to be d6tributed amongst the men for the purchase of the necessary articles. The Mayor received the following telegram in reply Cheque received quite safe. Myself and men very grateful. Leaving here to-day for Aldershot. Leave Liverpool tc-rnorrow (Thursday) for South Africa."•••••BUCKLEY.
