div.head: Messrs. Crosfields' Volunteers.
div.p: Messrs. Crosfields' Volunteers.

Privates Abbott and flassall, two of the Vo:unteers for the front, attended at Bank Quay Soap Works on Tuesday evening to receiva a hearty "send-off " from their fillow-workers. In the presence of a very large gathering, representatives of all departments,Mr George Cresfield, in the unavoidable absence ef the directors, presented to each man a purse of £5, contributed by the directors, managers, officers, and workpeople, and wished them, in the name of all, a prosperous journey and safe return. The works band at intervals played Rule Britannia," "Acid Lang Syne," and" God save the Queen," after which they escorted the Volunteers along Sa.nloy-street. Thirteen men employed by Messrs Cresfield have now left for the front, ten Reservists, one St. John Ambulance and two Volunteers.

div.head: Presentation to Whitecross Workmen.
div.p: Presentation to Whitecross Workmen.

Several of the works managers and employes of the Whitecress Works met on Tuesday afternoon for the purpose of making presentations to Corporal J, J. Houghton and Privates T. Cortess and W. Wadsworth. of the Warrington Volunteers, who have been accepted for active service at the front, and who were lately employed at the works.—Mr. Faischaw, works manager, in the course of a shorc speech remarked that he was very pleased to bear that the men had taken such an interest in the welfare of the Empire. They had been faithful servants at their work, and he was sure they would be as faithful to their country.—Mr. Carson, managing director, also said a few words. He assured corporalHoughton,who has a wife and family,that they would be well looked after while he was away. —Mr. Charnock, wire manager, then presented each man with a purse of gold. Os the purn was inscribed the name of the recipient.

div.head: Wanted to go to the Front.
div.p: Wanted to go to the Front.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday. John Gillens, a stranger, was charged with travelling on the Cneshire Lines Railway from Stockport to Warrington on the 18th inst. without paying the fare.—A ticket col- lector said that prisoner was found in a 3rd class corn- partmsnt in Vie 10-17 train from Stockport the previous night. At first be said he did not know where he got in the train but he had paid 7id fare tend ultimately said he had corne from Stockport and paid 4id. On wiring to Stockport it was ascertainel that no ticket bad been issued to the prisoner.—Prisoner : I wanted to go to Liverpool to volunteer for the front.—The Chairman : Couldn't you volunteer without going to Liverpool if you were in such a hurry P--The prisoner : No sir. I thought it was the headquarters of the volunteers.—The Chairman : I think you -canted to have a cheap ride. (Laughter.)—A fine of 53 and costs with the alternative of 7 days' imprisonment was imposed.
The Late Mr. John Fowler of the Ancient Order of Foresters.

On Sunday afternoon the remains of Bro. John Fowler were borne to their last resting place with great regret by the members of this district. Bro Fowler joined the court Marquis of Bute of the Bristol United District on November sth 1864. at which court for a period of four years he was a use- ful raember. For the services that he rendered, he was elected as the Chief Ranger. He left Bristol in search of employment, which he obtained at Leeds on the railway. He was transferred to Warringten in 1873, and during his residence here he has taken an active part in working for the Order. He has induced over 100 young men to join Court" War- rington" No. 430 for which that Court presented him with a Foresters Jewel. For eleven years he has been a collector of the Foresters Burial Society an 1 in this capacity he proved himself to be of great use to the Order. He was never content unless he was rendering some good service for his fellow men. He was a true hearted Forester always doing what he could for the interest of the Order.—His- death in the prime of life (54 years) is greatly mourned. He was carried to his grave with tokens of sympa- thy and regret by his brethern in Forestry. He was resoe.cted by all who knew him, and his genial face will be greatly missed. Us was for 15 yeirs timekeeper at Bewsey Forge where, he was held in great esteem and he was also a very useful member of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

PEARL LIFE ASSURANCE COMPANY, LTD. • ANNUAL REPORT FOR THE YEAR ENDING DECEMBER 31eT,1899. Presented at the Thirty-Sixth Annual General Meeting, held at the Offices of the Company, London Bridge, City, 8.0., Friday, February, 16th. 1900. In presenting the Report and Statement of Accounts for the year, your Directors have great pleasure in calling attention to the fact that from every point of view the success achieved by the Cempany during this period, exceeds anything previously recorded. The increase in Premium Income is for the first time above £106,000 in the year, it having reached the sum of i 10,371 ; while the increase in savings has grown by more than 36 per cent. and attained last year the large sum of 2158.170. The Accumulated Funds of the Company at the date of Issuing this Report exceed £1,000,C01. The Directors are satisfied that these tabulated results will prove as gratifying to the Shareholders and Staff as to them- selves, and they consider the work being done gives every indication that the gool results new recorded will be sur- passed by still greater accessions of business in the near future. In the Ordinary Branch the Premium Income for 1899 amounted to £79,687, being an increase of £15,806 ever that of the previous year. During the last three years the income in this branch has been nearly doubled. The Premiums on New Policies issued during the year amount to £29,936 7s. 6d., assuring the sum of £725,598. The Interim Valuation which has just been made by Mr R. M. Moore, A.1.A., up to December, 1899, shows a surplus of £147,099. 'The Directors recommend that the sum of 2138,352 be car- ried forward, leaving £10,747 to be distributed among the Participating Policy-holders. INCOME. The total income for the year amounted to £764.262 15s id, being an increase of £111,442 11s. 2d. ever that of last year. PREMIUMS (DECEMBER, 1899). The Premium Income on the Policies in force on the Com- pany's books, including 832,756 new Policies issued during the year, amounted to £832,483 Bs. 9d. CLAIMS. The Company has paid 40.860 Life Claims and Matured Endowments during the year, amounting with Bonuses, to £255,423 3s 7d, which, added to the sums previously paid in claims since the establishment of the Company, make a total of £2,442,821 19s 3d. ACCUMULATED FUNDS. The Assurance Funds, with capital paid up, now amount to £998,112 ss. 10d., showing an increase tor the year of £164,550 5s 3d. The Directors again cordially thank the Staff of the Com- pany for the continued care, zeal and abilltv,with which they have devoted their time and attention to the Company's Interest during the year. By Order, P. 3. FOLEY, Managing Director. See Reports and Opinions of the Press as to the remarkable progress made by the Company. Wanted, additional repre- sentatives in all districts. CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. MEMORANDUM ON TUBERCULOSIS IN CATTLE. In view of the prevalence of tuberculosis among dairy Cattle, and the danger of milk contamination arising therefrom, the attention of dairy farmers, eowkeepers, purveyors of milk and others is called to the following facts and recommendations. Tuberculosis, kno—n also as consumption, wasting and pining, is an infectious disease communicable from animals to man, and from one animal to another. The disease is spread by means of minute organisms, termed tubercle bacilli, which are ejected by diseased animals in coughing, and are also contained in the milk, in the discharge from the mouth and nose, and in the manure. Tnese bacilli are capable of prolonged vitality in a dry state, and may render air, food, or drink infective. The symptoms of tuberculosis, except in an advanced stage, are too ill-defined to permit of its detection in the ordinary way, but by the judicious employment of the tuberculin test, cattle affected with the disense in any stage may ordinarily be distinguished from those not so affected. Animals found to be suffering from tuberculosis either by the tuberculin test or otherwise, should be promptly separated from healthy stock. A carefully made parti- tion, well covered with tarred felt, to divide a shed into two parts, will euffice. Animals found to be in a low and wasted condition should be slaughtered and buried. ! A considerable quantity of milk which is sold to the public contains tubercle bacilli, and persons who drink this in an uncooked condition incur risk of infection. In a small pronertion of eases tubercle bacilli may be de- tected in milk by microscopic examination, and such milk is always highly dangerous. It ought to be clearly , understood, iaowever, that failure to detect the bacilli by microscopic examination of milk is not reliable ' evidence that such milk is free from tubercle bacilli. Milk from cows affected with disease of the udder should not be used for human consumption, or fed to calves, hut destroyed or buried. Tubercular disease of the udder ought always to be suspected when a painless , hard lump, slowly enlarging can be detected in one or more of the quarters. Bat milk may contain tuberoule bacilli even when drawn from an udder which appears to be perfectly healthy. Calves from cows affected with tuberculosis should be removed from the dam at birth and reared on milk from healthy stock. Figs and fowls suffering from wasting disease should be excluded from yards, sheds and pastures containing dairy cattle, unless the former have been certified free from tuberculosis by a veterinary surgeon. Dairy cattle should be kept in the open air as much as possible; and when they are oat ot the bytes, windows, ventilators and doors should be open to the fullest ex- tent. Overcrowding should be guarded against ; and byres should be well ventilated, lighted and kept cleaned. Byres should be drained by channels, delivering on suitable gully-traps outside the buildings. The drains should be kept in good ordcr, and flushed daily. Man- gers and fittings should be washed and disinfected, and the byre-walls should be periodically lime-washed. Calves at grass should not be pastured with mulch cows, or be allowed to run over fields where the latter habitually graze, unless the mulch cows have passed the tuberculin test. No one suffering from consumption should be allowed to take part in the management of dairy cattle, or in any branch of dairy work. Consumers of milk are especially recommended to raise the temperature of milk to boiling point before using it unless their milk supply be derived from cattle tested with tuberculin and passed. FRANCIS VAGUER. County Medical Officer of Health. JAMES LAITHWOOD, Chief Veterinary Inspector. December 22nd, 18119. NOTE.—Additional copies of this Memorandum can he obtained from Messrs.
